weeks.title: Love Is a Decision and an Action
weeks.theme: Without love, all the talent and giving in the world amounts to nothing.
group: Read 1 Cor 13:1–3. Why do talent and giving without love amount to nothing?
The last time you gave of yourself, was it out of love, or out of duty or fear?
In which relationship do you want to turn love into visible action this week?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, share with a companion: this week I learned that love is action, and one thing I want to do is… Ask them to pray for you, and pass “love is a decision and an action” on to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, find a friend or family member and plan a time to “say love through action”: cook a meal, walk with them for a while, or write a card. Afterward, write down: As I did it, what was the motive in my heart?

lessons.title: Without Love, You Are Nothing
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie was great at serving: every week she led worship, organized events, and remembered everyone’s birthday. But the person she was dating said, “I always feel like you’re getting a job done, not loving me.” Xiaojie was deeply hurt, yet it also stopped her in her tracks.

Paul says, “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.” (1 Cor 13:1) Talent, gifts, and service, without love, are left as nothing but noise.

Love is not the highs and lows of emotion, nor how much you do, but your whole person turned toward the good of the other. The easiest thing in a relationship is to do many “things”; the hardest is to do them with love.

This week, we don’t start by asking whether the other person loves me, but by asking: is there love in what I do?

Xiaojie later learned to pray quietly before each time of service, asking herself: Who am I doing this for?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: every one of his actions came out of love for people. The Bible is my standard: without love, I am nothing. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he pours God’s love into our hearts. A person living for self gives in order to be needed; a person living in selflessness lets Christ’s love flow out from within.
think: According to 1 Cor 13:1, what is talent without love like?
Is my giving sometimes for the sake of being affirmed or needed, or truly for the other person’s good?
How can I do one thing today with love, and not just out of duty?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often do many things and forget why I do them. Purify my motives, so that I act not to be seen or needed, but only for love. Holy Spirit, pour your love into my heart, so that my service and giving carry your love. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, before doing something you normally do (replying to a message, helping out, keeping someone company), pause for three seconds and pray in your heart: Lord, let your love come through me. Then do it.
lessons.quick: Without love, all the talent and giving in the world is just noise.
text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.

lessons.title: Love in Deed and Truth
lessons.hear:
Kai often told the person he was dating, “I love you, and I’ll love you forever.” But he was often late for the times they had set, and often forgot what he had promised. She said, “Your words are sweet, but I can’t see them.”

John writes, “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18) Love needs to be spoken, and it also needs to be seen; and seen in “truth,” not put on as a performance.

Deeds turn love into something that can be touched: being on time, keeping your word, listening closely, remembering the small things the other person has said. Truth means that what you say and what you do match, with nothing exaggerated and nothing hidden.

Love is not one grand announcement, but a string of small, reliable choices.

Kai began writing down what he had promised and finishing each thing, one by one. She didn’t change her view right away, but he knew that love has to be proved over time.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his love was shown in action; he washed the disciples’ feet and died for us. The Bible is my standard: don’t love in word only, but in deed and truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes what I say and what I do match. A love of self depends on feelings; a love of selflessness depends on the decision Christ gives.
think: According to 1 John 3:18, how are we to love one another?
Do I often say more than I do? How might the other person feel about that?
Which small thing I promised can I finish today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you love me by your actions, not only with words. Help me do what I say, without exaggeration or falseness. Holy Spirit, remind me of the small promises I have forgotten, so that I love people with truth and deeds. Make me faithful in small things too. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, finish one small thing you promised someone but put off, and then send one specific sentence: I remember you said…, thank you.
lessons.quick: Love must be seen: keep your word, in deed and truth.
text: My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.title: Love Without Hypocrisy
lessons.hear:
To make the other person happy, Xiaoyu said “sure” to everything, and even for movies she didn’t like and opinions she didn’t agree with, she said, “Me too.” After a while, he asked, “What do you actually like?” Xiaoyu couldn’t answer.

Paul says, “Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.” (Rom 12:9) Love is not people-pleasing, nor is it suppression. Real love has both honesty and discernment: drawing near to what should be drawn near to, and staying away from what should be avoided.

False love often comes out of fear: fear of being rejected, fear of being left, fear of conflict. But love driven by fear is not love; it is self-protection.

Love without hypocrisy means telling the truth, and telling it gently. In a relationship, we don’t need to pretend; because we are accepted by God, we can be real.

Xiaoyu later learned to say, “I don’t really like this movie, but I really like watching it with you.” Telling the truth, it turns out, can be very gentle.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is full of grace and truth, neither pleasing people nor hurting them. The Bible is my standard: let love be without hypocrisy; abhor what is evil and cling to what is good. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he enables us to speak honestly in love. A love of self is a safety that is put on; a love of selflessness is being real in Christ.
think: According to Rom 12:9, how must love not be?
In my relationship, have I pretended to agree or pretended nothing was wrong because I was afraid of losing it?
Can I say one true thought today in a gentle way?
lessons.speak: Lord, I am often afraid of being rejected, so I pretend and try to please. Heal my fear, so that I feel safe in your love. Holy Spirit, give me the courage to be honest, and a gentle mouth, so that my love is without hypocrisy. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, with someone you trust, honestly share one small true thought or feeling (it doesn’t have to be with the person you’re dating), in a gentle tone: Actually, I prefer…
lessons.quick: Love without hypocrisy: speaking honestly in grace.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.

lessons.title: Love Is Obedience
lessons.hear:
When Xiaoen first started dating, he often said, “Whatever you want is fine; I’ll go along.” Then one day he found that she wanted him to give up serving. He struggled: if I love her, should I listen to everything she says?

Jesus said, “If you love me, keep my commandments.” (John 14:15) This verse speaks of love for Jesus: if you love him, you obey him. The one we obey is the Lord, not any one person.

Only someone who loves the Lord has a steady direction for loving others. What people ask of us sometimes agrees with God’s heart and sometimes doesn’t; we obey God and also respect people, but we don’t put anyone in God’s place.

It must be made especially clear: this verse cannot be used to demand that anyone submit to another person’s control, belittling, or harm. Obedience in loving someone comes from freedom, not from fear.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he obeyed the Father out of love, not because he was forced. The Bible is my standard: if you love me, keep my commandments. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes us love God’s word. Let people be people and let God be God: obeying God is not submitting to people’s control. When we let Jesus be King, we are not pushed around by people’s demands.
think: According to John 14:15, how does love for Jesus show itself?
Is my obedience out of love, or out of fear?
Am I putting someone’s expectations before God’s word?
lessons.speak: Jesus, I love you and I am willing to keep your words. Help me discern which is your voice and which is human pressure. Holy Spirit, help me obey you, and give me courage in my relationships to say the no that needs to be said. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, pick one of Jesus’ commands (for example: love one another), write it on a sticky note, find a chance today to follow it specifically, and write down the result tonight.
lessons.quick: Loving the Lord means obeying the Lord; obeying the Lord is not submitting to people’s control.
text: If you love me, keep my commandments.

lessons.title: Pursue Love
lessons.hear:
Yu wanted to have love, but often just waited for love to come. He said, “When the right person shows up, I’ll love.” A year went by, and not much in his life had changed.

Paul tells the church, “Follow after love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts.” (1 Cor 14:1) To pursue love is a verb. Love is not only a feeling you wait for; it is also a life that is pursued: learning, practicing, failing, and practicing again.

You don’t need someone to date first in order to pursue love. You can practice with family, friends, and coworkers: patience, respect, honesty, forgiveness. When love becomes your life, you have love to give in any relationship.

This week, we look back: without love, we are nothing; love is action; love must be honest; love is obeying the Lord; love must be pursued. A person living for self asks, “Who will love me?” A person living in selflessness asks, “How can I love others?”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he took the initiative to go to people and love them. The Bible is my standard: follow after love. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he bears the fruit of love. This week’s review: where is the self in me? How does God hold me up? Let Jesus be King, and let all the glory go to God. Humility is returning to a person’s rightful place, letting people be people and God be God.
think: According to 1 Cor 14:1, how are we to treat love?
This week, where did I see the self in me? How did God hold me up in it?
In which relationship can I begin to practice love proactively?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for teaching me what love is this week. Forgive me for often waiting for love to come without pursuing it. Holy Spirit, help me begin practicing love proactively from today, so that in every relationship I can show Christ. Glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: the self I saw this week; God’s support; one person I will practice love toward. Today, take the initiative to do one small thing for this person.
lessons.quick: Love is to be pursued: starting today, practice it in one relationship.
text: Follow after love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.

weeks.keyText: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing. If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.

weeks.title: Patient and Kind
weeks.theme: Love begins with patience and kindness; it does not envy and does not brag.
group: Read 1 Cor 13:4. What qualities does love have? Which one challenges you the most?
What was the last time you felt envious or wanted to brag, and what was it about?
In which relationship do you want to take the first step with kindness and humility this week?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a companion and tell each other: this week what I most need God to change is… Pray for each other for three minutes, and pass “humility sets off humility” on to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, get together with two friends for a “practice of praise”: each person names one specific strength of each of the other two, saying only what is true. Afterward, each of you write down: When I was praised and when I praised someone, what did I feel?

lessons.title: Patient
lessons.hear:
Zhe’s girlfriend often forgot to reply to messages because of work. At first Zhe said it was fine, then he began to turn cold, and finally he said, “I’ve waited long enough.” In fact, he hadn’t waited very long; he had simply never told her how he felt.

Paul says, “Love is patient and is kind.” (1 Cor 13:4) To be “patient” means to be slow to anger. It is not suppression, and it is not pretending nothing is wrong; it is still giving the other person time and space when you have been offended.

Be careful: patience does not mean tolerating harm. If the other person’s behavior is controlling, humiliating, or violent, that is not a small matter to be put up with but something that calls for seeking help (see the safety reminder in this course). Being patient refers to facing weakness and imperfection, not facing harm.

This is how God is with us: he is patient with us for a long time, waiting for us to turn back.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: even when the disciples were slow again and again and weak again and again, he stayed patient and kept teaching them. The Bible is my standard: love is patient and kind. The Holy Spirit is my guide: patience is among the fruit he bears. A person living for self is easily impatient, because they center on their own timing; a person living in selflessness follows God’s rhythm.
think: According to 1 Cor 13:4, what two qualities does love have?
With which kind of weakness am I least patient? What am I thinking at that moment?
Is my patience right now out of love, or out of suppression? What do I need to say honestly?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are patient with me, and I want to love people this way. Keep me from being hasty or cold, and help me say honestly what I feel. Holy Spirit, bear the fruit of patience in me, and give me wisdom to tell the difference between weakness and harm. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you meet a person or situation that makes you impatient, take three deep breaths first and say in your heart: Lord, give me your patience. Then choose one gentle sentence to respond with.
lessons.quick: Being patient means being slow to anger; but it does not mean tolerating harm.
text: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,

lessons.title: Treat Others with Kindness
lessons.hear:
After an argument with her boyfriend, Xiaoting didn’t speak to him for three days. She thought: if he really loved me, he should apologize first. He was thinking the same thing. Both were waiting for the other to bow first.

Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Eph 4:32) Kindness means giving out goodwill first, rather than waiting for the other person to change first.

“Just as God also in Christ forgave you” is the source of the power: we don’t forgive because the other person deserves it, but because we have first been forgiven.

It must be made clear: kindness and forgiveness do not equal restoring trust right away. If the other person has hurt you, you can first let go of it in your heart, but trust needs the other person’s repentance and time to be rebuilt (this course will discuss it in detail later).

Kindness begins with a soft word and a small act of taking the initiative.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he asked forgiveness for the very people who crucified him, giving kindness first. The Bible is my standard: be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving each other. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he places Christ’s kindness in our hearts. A person living for self waits for the other to bow first; a person living in selflessness humbles themselves first and sets off humility.
think: According to Eph 4:32, why are we to forgive each other?
Am I waiting for the other person to apologize or change first right now? What am I holding on to?
What small kind thing can I do first for this relationship?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for forgiving me in Christ. Make me willing to give kindness first, without waiting for the other person to bow first. Give me wisdom to discern what to let go of and what needs a boundary. Holy Spirit, soften my heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, take the initiative with someone you’ve had a little friction with and say one soft sentence: Thank you for yesterday…, or: I’d like to talk with you properly. If there is a safety concern, pray for them instead, and don’t reach out.
lessons.quick: Only those who have been forgiven first know kindness; forgiveness does not equal restoring trust right away.
text: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Not Envious
lessons.hear:
Xiaohao saw that a friend’s partner was very good at caring for people, and he couldn’t help thinking: why isn’t mine like that? At every gathering he kept comparing, and when he got home he became more and more critical of his own partner.

Solomon says, “The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.” (Prov 14:30) Envy is not just an emotion; it eats away at a person from the inside. It quietly keeps us from seeing what we have, and lets us see only what others have.

There are two kinds of envy in dating: one is envying other people’s relationships; the other is feeling insecure about your own partner and wanting to control, check up on, or restrict them. The first needs gratitude; the second needs security in God.

It must be said specifically: if envy turns into monitoring, tracking, or limiting the other person’s social life, it is no longer love, and needs to be faced honestly and help sought.

A heart at peace is a heart that has been settled by God’s love.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he had complete security in the Father’s love and did not need to compare himself with anyone. The Bible is my standard: a heart at peace gives life to the body, but envy rots the bones. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he brings peace. A person living for self looks for security in comparison; a person living in selflessness finds security in God’s love.
think: What does Prov 14:30 compare envy to?
What do I most easily envy or compare? What insecurity lies behind it?
Can I give God thanks today for three things I have?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often look at what others have and forget what I have been given. Heal the insecurity in my heart, so that I find security in your love. Help me rejoice in others’ blessings, and give thanks for my own calling. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things I have, and thank God and one person for one of them. Spend less time today scrolling social media or looking at other people’s relationship updates.
lessons.quick: Envy eats away at a person; God’s love quiets the heart.
text: The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.

lessons.title: Not Bragging
lessons.hear:
Xun wanted to pursue a sister in Christ, so he often brought up his accomplishments in the group chat: I went on a mission trip, I lead a small group, I’ve read this many chapters. Hearing this, the sister grew more and more distant.

Proverbs says, “Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.” (Prov 27:2) Bragging is trying to trade your own goodness for other people’s attention. Behind it is often a fear: fear that I’m not good enough, fear that others won’t see me.

Bragging in dating may be showing off achievements, showing off spirituality, or showing off popularity. But love looks at the other person, not at yourself.

Not bragging is not false modesty, and it is not putting yourself down. It is being at ease being the person God made, letting your actions speak, and letting others do the praising.

When we no longer need to be seen, we have eyes to see others.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the Son of God, yet did not boast for himself, but gave glory only to the Father. The Bible is my standard: let another man praise you, and not your own mouth. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he fixes our eyes on Christ, not on ourselves. A person living for self needs to be seen; a person living in selflessness lets Jesus be seen.
think: How does Prov 27:2 tell us to handle praise?
Do I try to show myself off in front of others? What am I afraid of behind it?
How can I pass praise on to God, or to others, today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often want to be seen and praised. Help me know that I am already seen by you and loved by you. Forgive my bragging, so that my eyes see the good in others, and give all the glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, in conversation, deliberately leave out one of your accomplishments, ask the other person one more question, and listen to the whole answer without rushing to reply.
lessons.quick: Not bragging: when we don’t need to be seen, we have eyes to see others.
text: Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.

lessons.title: Do Not Seek Empty Glory
lessons.hear:
This week, we walked together through the love of 1 Cor 13:4: patient, kind, not envious, not bragging. Each one is showing us the self in our hearts.

In Philippians, Paul says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” (Phil 2:3) “Empty glory” is glory with no weight: being envied, being praised, being needed. All of these will pass away.

“Counting others better than yourself” is not low self-worth, but seeing what God is doing in others and rejoicing in it.

Perhaps this week you saw many of your shortcomings. Don’t be discouraged; recognizing the self is the beginning of being enlightened. God is kind; he doesn’t shine his light in order to condemn, but to heal.

Humility overcomes pride, and humility sets off humility.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. The Bible is my standard: in humility, count others better than yourself. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us recognize the self in us, and gives grace to change. Self is leaving your place and grasping at power; humility is laying down power and returning to your place.
think: What does Phil 2:3 say we must not do? With what attitude must we do things?
This week, where did I see the self in me? How did God hold me up in it?
In which relationship can I first use humility to set off humility?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for shining your light on me this week. Forgive my envy and bragging, so that I have a humble mind and count others better than myself. Holy Spirit, renew me every day, so that in every relationship I first use humility to set off humility. Glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: one self I saw this week; how God held me up; one act of humility I will practice. Today, find a chance to sincerely praise someone.
lessons.quick: In humility, count others better than yourself; humility sets off humility.
text: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;

weeks.title: Not Seeking Its Own Way
weeks.theme: Love does not take; it puts the other person’s good first.
group: Read 1 Cor 13:5. What are the expressions of love there? Which one do you most need to learn?
Think of the last time you got angry easily or dug up an old offense. What expectation was behind it?
This week, for which person do you want to do one specific thing that puts their good first?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday, share with a companion what you saw of self in “not seeking its own way” this week, and ask him or her to pray for you. Pass on “love that keeps no record” to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, do a “needs and expectations” exercise with a companion or your group. Each person writes down three expectations they have in relationships, then says them aloud using the pattern “I feel…, and I need…”. Practice saying your needs without anger.

lessons.title: Not Seeking Its Own Way
lessons.hear:
Whenever Sen and his girlfriend decided where to go on the weekend, it was always the same sentence: “Let’s go where I want to go.” He didn’t see anything wrong with that, because, he said, he was doing it for the good of both of them. After a while, his girlfriend said, “I feel like I’m just an accessory in your life.”

Paul says love “doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil.” (1 Cor 13:5) The first check of love is motive: for whose good am I doing this?

“Not seeking its own way” doesn’t mean you can’t have needs, and it doesn’t mean suppressing yourself. It means not putting your own good first, and certainly not letting it become the only thing that counts. In a healthy relationship, both people are seen, and both people’s needs have a place.

A person living for self asks, “What’s in it for me?” A selfless person asks, “What is good for us, and for God’s kingdom?”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he did not seek his own pleasure but fulfilled the Father’s will, and he gave himself up for our good. The Bible is my standard: love does not seek its own way. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us a heart that cares for others. Self is centered on itself; selflessness lets Jesus live within and see the needs of others.
think: What does 1 Cor 13:5 say love does not seek?
In my recent decisions, have I often used my own convenience as the standard?
For whom can I make a choice today that puts their good first?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often think about myself more than about others. Forgive my selfishness, and teach me to see other people’s needs. Holy Spirit, give me a heart like yours, so that in every choice I ask: what is good for people and for your kingdom? Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you make a decision (what to eat, where to go, how to arrange your time), first ask what the other person wants, then offer your own opinion, and respect each other’s needs.
lessons.quick: Love does not seek its own way, and it does not erase your own needs.
text: doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;

lessons.title: Look Also to the Things of Others
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie and her coworker Xiaoan were in charge of an event together. Every time, Xiaojie thought only about her own part and never asked what Xiaoan needed. It wasn’t until Xiaoan collapsed from exhaustion that Xiaojie realized: I had only been looking after my own things.

Paul says, “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Phil 2:4) Notice that he says “not just looking,” not “not looking.” We have our own things, and our own responsibilities. But it can’t be only our own things.

In dating, this verse is especially practical: when the other person is busy, tired, or sad, does anyone notice? When we begin to pay attention to other people’s situations, love begins.

“Also looking” widens our vision: from seeing only ourselves, to seeing the other person, and then to seeing the people God has placed around us.

Later, before every meeting, Xiaojie began by asking, “How are you today?” That one sentence changed the atmosphere of the team.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he always saw people’s needs, including the hungry, the sick, and the forgotten. The Bible is my standard: look also to the things of others. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he widens our vision. The view of self holds only me; the view of selflessness holds God and people.
think: What does Phil 2:4 say we should look to besides our own things?
Who around me has been going through a hard time that I haven’t noticed?
Today, can I reach out to one person and ask, “How have you been?”
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you always saw people’s needs. Open my eyes so that I look not only to my own things but also to the things of others. Holy Spirit, help me notice, in the middle of my busyness, the person who needs care, and make me a channel of your love. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, take the initiative to ask a friend or family member, “How have you been? Is there anything I can help with?” Then listen attentively for ten minutes without rushing to give advice.
lessons.quick: Not just looking to our own things, but also to the things of others.
text: each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.title: One Who Is Slow to Anger Has Great Understanding
lessons.hear:
When Hao was dating, he would flare up whenever the other person was even a little late replying to a message. He said, “I just care too much.” But she said, “Being next to you feels like walking a tightrope.”

Solomon says, “He who is slow to anger has great understanding.” (Prov 14:29) Anger itself is not necessarily sin, but being quick to anger is dangerous. It shows that our heart is not yet under God’s management.

Anger is often a signal: I have an expectation that has not been met. The problem is that we often treat expectations as rights and use anger to punish the other person.

A safety reminder: if anger has already brought shouting, throwing things, threats, or physical harm, this is not just “a bad temper.” It is harm that must be dealt with. Please seek help from a pastor and from professionals (see “I Need Help”).

A wise person stops before getting angry and asks himself: what do I really need?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he could be angry without sinning, and his anger was for the sake of justice and people’s good. The Bible is my standard: one who is slow to anger has great understanding. The Holy Spirit is my guide: the fruit he bears includes self-control. The anger of self is to defend myself; the anger of selflessness is handed over to God.
think: What does Prov 14:29 say is true of the person who is slow to anger?
When I get angry, what unmet expectation is behind it?
Next time I get angry, what small step can I use to pause first?
lessons.speak: Lord, my emotions are often faster than I am. Give me a spirit of self-control, so that before I get angry I stop and come to you. Heal the wounded places in my heart, and teach me to voice my needs in ways that don’t hurt people. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you feel angry, pause for ten seconds, take a deep breath, and say in your heart, “Lord, what do I need?” Then say it using the pattern “I feel…, and I need…”.
lessons.quick: Being slow to anger is wise; if there is harm, please seek help.
text: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.

lessons.title: Keeping No Record of Wrongs
lessons.hear:
Fan and his girlfriend got into an argument over a recent matter, and he dug up something from three years ago in one breath: “You did the same thing that time too!” His girlfriend said, “Didn’t we already talk about that?”

“Takes no account of evil” (1 Cor 13:5) carries the sense of “keeping no ledger” in the original. Some people carry a ledger in their heart, recording each of the other person’s mistakes, and when needed, they pull it out.

The psalm says, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins.” (Ps 103:10) God has no such ledger. In Christ, he has already wiped out our sins.

Keeping no ledger does not mean forgetting or denying the hurt. Some harm needs to be taken seriously, needs boundaries, and may even require leaving. Keeping no ledger means this: I no longer use the past to punish the present.

If you are the one who was hurt, please don’t feel responsible to stop keeping count quickly. You have the right to seek help and to take time.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he bore the debt of our sins and does not bring it up again. The Bible is my standard: he has not dealt with us according to our sins. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps us let go of old ledgers. A person living for self keeps a ledger to protect himself; a selfless person hands the ledger over to God. When Jesus is King, the old ledger has a place to go.
think: How does Ps 103:10 describe the way God treats us?
What “old ledger” do I carry in my heart that often gets pulled out during arguments?
Which old matter can I hand over to God today, and no longer use to punish the other person?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you have not dealt with me according to my sins. Heal my wounded heart so that I can hand my old ledger over to you. Give me wisdom to tell what needs to be let go and what needs boundaries and help. Holy Spirit, set my heart free. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one old matter you have not been able to let go of, pray and entrust it to God, and then decide: will I let it go, or do I need to ask someone to help me deal with it? Don’t carry it alone.
lessons.quick: Keeping no record of wrongs: don’t use the past to punish the present; but harm needs to be taken seriously.
text: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.
He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.
He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.

lessons.title: Love One Another Earnestly
lessons.hear:
This week, we walked through 1 Cor 13:5: not seeking its own way, looking also to others, being slow to anger, and keeping no record of wrongs. Each one invites us to move from self toward selflessness.

Peter says, “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” (1 Pet 4:8) “Earnest” means stretched out and focused, like an athlete straining every muscle. Love is not passive; it takes effort.

“Covers a multitude of sins” does not mean hiding sin, pretending nothing happened, or concealing harm. It means that in love, we don’t broadcast other people’s weaknesses, we don’t go around talking about their faults, and we choose to treat those who have failed with grace.

A safety principle: what love covers is not violence, abuse, or crime. Those things need to be spoken about and dealt with.

What did you see this week? How did God support you?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he paid the price for our sins without shaming us. The Bible is my standard: above all, love one another earnestly. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us strength to love. This week’s review: where is the self in me? How did God support me? Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: What does 1 Pet 4:8 say is most important?
This week, where did I see self in me? How did God support me in it?
In which relationship do I need to love earnestly, and not only feel love?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for teaching me this week. Forgive my selfishness in not seeking others’ good, and my quickness to anger. Holy Spirit, give me strength to love earnestly, not to broadcast others’ weaknesses, and not to condone harm. To you be the glory. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write: the self I saw this week; God’s support; and for whom I will love earnestly. Do one specific thing today, such as sending an encouraging message.
lessons.quick: Love earnestly: what love covers is weakness, not harm.
text: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.

weeks.keyText: doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;

weeks.title: Bearing All Things; Love Never Fails
weeks.theme: Love bears and believes, but love is not the same as condoning, and certainly not the same as staying in harm.
group: Read 1 Cor 13:6–7. How does love both “rejoice with the truth” and “bear all things”?
Have you ever put up with something you shouldn’t have, out of fear of conflict?
This week, which trustworthy person do you need to contact, to tell them about something that is troubling you?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday, share with a companion: have I seen any warning signs? Ask him or her to pray for you, and pass on “bear with weakness, but don’t condone harm” to a friend who needs it.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, hold a “warning signs and resources” gathering with two companions: read “I Need Help” together, save each other’s contact information, and pray for one another. This doesn’t require that you be dating anyone; it is preparation for everyone.

lessons.title: Bears All Things, Believes All Things
lessons.hear:
When Fang heard “bears all things,” she struggled inside. The person she was dating often put her down, and she told herself: love bears all things, so I have to put up with it. As a result, she became less and less happy.

Paul says, “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.” (1 Cor 13:7) This verse describes the attitude of love. It is not a command to stay in harm.

“Bears” originally means “to cover, to carry.” It means being patient with people’s weaknesses, such as imperfect habits, a momentary mistake, or immaturity that is still growing.

But bearing is not condoning. Humiliation, control, threats, and violence are not weaknesses to be borne; they are harm that must be faced. While we bear with weakness, we also need to protect ourselves, and when necessary, leaving danger is permitted.

Love bears with weakness, and it also honors the truth.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he accepted weak people but not sin; he is full of grace and also truth. The Bible is my standard: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us wisdom to tell weakness from harm. The bearing of self comes from people-pleasing; the bearing of selflessness comes from Christ’s love and walks together with truth.
think: Which four “all things” does 1 Cor 13:7 describe in love?
Has my past “bearing” actually been suppression, fear, or people-pleasing?
In which situation do I need to tell “weakness” and “harm” apart?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me wisdom to tell what is weakness and what is harm. Help me bear with people’s weaknesses, and also give me courage to protect myself. Holy Spirit, guide me so that in love I never leave the truth. Please also guard my heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, in your journal, make two columns: “Weaknesses I can bear with” and “Behaviors that need boundaries or help.” If the second column has anything in it, please tell a trusted pastor or friend today.
lessons.quick: Love bears with weakness but does not condone harm; leaving danger is permitted.
text: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.

lessons.title: Love Never Fails
lessons.hear:
Xiaozhe said, “Will love fade someday?” His parents were divorced, and he found it hard to believe in “forever.”

Paul says, “Love never fails.” (1 Cor 13:8) He goes on to say that prophecies, tongues, and knowledge will all pass away, but love will not.

This is not a guarantee that every relationship on earth will last. It says that the essence of love comes from God and is eternal, and God never changes. The love we have received is not kept up by us but by him.

Some relationships end because of harm, and some because they were not a good fit. That doesn’t mean love has failed, and it doesn’t mean you have failed. The source of love is God, and his love is always enough.

In human love, we learn; in God’s love, we rest.

Later, Xiaozhe began writing down God’s grace each week, and slowly he saw that love had been there all along.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved the world and loved to the end. The Bible is my standard: love never fails. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he confirms in our hearts that God’s love never changes. A person living for self fears being left; a selfless person rests in God’s love that never fails. When Jesus is King, we can rest in him.
think: What does 1 Cor 13:8 say never fails?
Do I have doubts or fears about “lasting love”?
Where can I remember today that God’s love has never left me?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your love never fails. Heal my fear of “being left,” and let me find security in your unchanging love. Holy Spirit, help me believe that whatever happens in my relationships, you hold me tightly. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes writing down three times when “God did not leave me.” Thank God for one of them, and tell a friend about it.
lessons.quick: Love never fails, because the source of love is God.
text: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.

lessons.title: Does Not Rejoice in Unrighteousness, but Rejoices with the Truth
lessons.hear:
Wen’s girlfriend posted something inaccurate in the group chat. He knew it was wrong but didn’t want to say so, afraid of ruining the mood. He thought: love means bearing with people and not fussing over right and wrong.

Paul says love “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth.” (1 Cor 13:6) True love does not keep the peace by being vague. Love rejoices in the truth, and it rejoices in telling the truth.

Some people think love means not arguing and not speaking up. In fact, love sometimes needs to say, gently but firmly, “This isn’t right.”

But “telling the truth” is not the same as “blaming people.” Truth must be spoken in love, and love must stand within truth. Grace and truth are both essential.

If you find that the other person’s behavior has already hurt others, or hurt you, please don’t stay silent out of fear of conflict. That is not love for anyone.

Later, Wen found his courage and reminded her privately in a gentle tone, and the relationship became more real.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is full of grace and full of truth. The Bible is my standard: love does not rejoice in unrighteousness but rejoices with the truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit of truth, who guides us into all truth. The love of self uses silence to protect itself; the love of selflessness tells the truth in grace.
think: What does 1 Cor 13:6 say love rejoices in, and what does it not rejoice in?
Have I stayed silent, out of fear of conflict, when I shouldn’t have?
Next time I need to tell the truth, what tone and timing can I use?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the way, the truth, and the life. Help me delight in the truth and speak the truth in love. Give me courage and wisdom not to lie for the sake of peace, and not to hurt people for the sake of truth. Help me always remember your grace. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, find one truth you know needs to be said but have not yet said. Write three sentences (first something affirming, then the facts, then what you need), and practice with a trusted friend.
lessons.quick: Love rejoices with the truth: grace and truth are both essential.
text: doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;

lessons.title: A Prudent Person Sees Danger and Hides
lessons.hear:
Xiaomi felt uneasy about her boyfriend’s behavior: he often told her to delete certain friends. She had her doubts but told herself: I should trust him.

Solomon says, “A prudent man sees danger and hides himself,” while the simple go ahead and suffer for it. (Prov 22:3) Love “believes all things,” but believing is not the same as having no wisdom. Seeing danger and getting away from it is wise, not a lack of faith.

What does it mean to “see danger”? For example: being isolated, controlled, humiliated, threatened, forced to go against your own boundaries, or told to keep secrets. These are all signs of danger.

When you see them, please don’t talk yourself into believing, “It’s fine.” Tell a trusted person, such as a pastor, a counselor, or a friend, and seek help.

Avoiding danger is not a lack of love; it is taking responsibility for the life God has created.

Later, Xiaomi went to a pastor for counseling. It wasn’t easy, but it was the beginning of finding her peace again.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: sometimes he left a dangerous place, not out of cowardice but to act according to the Father’s timing. The Bible is my standard: a prudent person sees danger and hides. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us wisdom to discern danger. A person living for self ignores warning signs for fear of losing something; a selfless person entrusts safety to God and also takes responsibility for life.
think: How does Prov 22:3 distinguish the “prudent” from the “simple”?
Have I seen certain warning signs and talked myself into thinking they were fine?
Which trustworthy person can I ask to look at this together with me?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for giving me wisdom. Help me not to ignore warning signs and not to be afraid to seek help. Give me courage to protect myself when I need to. Holy Spirit, guide me to walk on a path of peace and safety. And keep me from being alone. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, read the “I Need Help” page of this course, and save the phone number or contact information of one trusted person in your phone. If anything is troubling you, contact him or her today.
lessons.quick: Seeing danger and getting away is wisdom; seeking help is courage.
text: A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.

lessons.title: Love Is the Fulfillment of the Law
lessons.hear:
This week, we walked through 1 Cor 13:6–8: love rejoices with the truth, bears, hopes, and endures all things, and never fails; and at the same time, the prudent see danger and hide.

Paul says, “Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” (Rom 13:8) Love is the one debt we always owe; every person deserves to be loved.

Love is not a new law but the fulfillment of the law. All the commandments are summed up in this one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love does not harm anyone, and it does not condone those who do.

Perhaps this week you found that your love often leans to one side: only bearing, without truth; or only truth, without kindness. God wants us to have both.

Where is the self in you? How did God support you?

Love is a debt we repay for a lifetime, and it is also a lifetime of joy.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he summed up the whole law as loving God and loving people. The Bible is my standard: whoever loves has fulfilled the law. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us love and also wisdom. This week’s review: where is the self in me? How did God support me? Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: What does Rom 13:8 say about the relationship between love and the law?
This week, where did I see self in me? How did God support me in it?
Does my love lean more toward “bearing” or more toward “truth”? Which side needs to be added?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for making love the fulfillment of the law. Forgive my one-sidedness, and let me have both grace and truth in love. Holy Spirit, renew me every day so that I have both patience and wisdom. The glory is yours. And help me rely on you every day. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write: the self I saw this week; God’s support; and which side of my love needs to be added. Today, do one thing to add the side that is lacking.
lessons.quick: Love is the fulfillment of the law; love has both grace and truth.
text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.

weeks.keyText: bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things. Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.

weeks.title: Love
weeks.theme: Loving as Jesus loved us is the first fruit the Spirit bears in us.
group: Read John 13:34–35. What is the standard of the new commandment?
When was the last time you felt God loving you through someone else, and in what way?
This week, for which person do you want to do one loving thing that bears the mark of Jesus?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday, share with a companion: who is the hardest person for me to love this week? Ask him or her to pray for you, and pass on “as I have loved you” to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, go with a companion or your group to visit, accompany, or serve someone in need (an elderly person, a sick person, someone who lives alone), turning love into visible action. Afterward, share: where did I see God’s love?

lessons.title: A New Commandment
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqi was known at church as an enthusiastic person, but she and a sister in her group had been in a cold war for half a year over a misunderstanding. She said, “I love everyone, except her.”

Jesus said, “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” (John 13:34) What is “new” about this commandment? What’s new is the standard: “Just as I have loved you.” It is not loving in the way we like, but loving in the way Jesus loves us.

Jesus’ love is washing the disciples’ feet, accepting weak people, and giving his life for our sins. This kind of love is far beyond our strength, so we need him to live in us.

The mark of a disciple is not our talent or our enthusiasm, but that we love one another. Love is the most persuasive testimony.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved to the end, all the way to the cross. The Bible is my standard: just as I have loved you, you also love one another. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he pours God’s love into our hearts so that we can love as Jesus loves. A person living for self loves by his own standard; a selfless person lets Christ’s love flow out from within.
think: What is the standard of the new commandment in John 13:34?
Who is the hardest person for me to love? Where is my heart stuck?
Today, how can I do one small, Jesus-like act of love for this person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want to love people the way you have loved me. Give me your love, not by my own strength, but by your living in me. Holy Spirit, help me to see your image even in the person who is hardest for me to love. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend three minutes praying for someone you find hard to get along with, asking God to bless him or her. Then choose to do one small thing that benefits that person, such as a greeting. If there is any safety concern, just pray.
lessons.quick: Jesus-style love: just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

lessons.title: Laying Down One’s Life for Friends
lessons.hear:
When Jie heard “lay down his life for his friends,” he felt he could never do it. He said, “It’s hard enough for me to get up early once for a friend, never mind lay down my life.”

Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” (John 15:13) Laying down your life is not only one death; it is a daily choice: spending time, spending energy, and setting aside your own convenience for the good of others.

Jesus himself is the best example: he laid down his life for his friends out of freedom, not compulsion.

We need to be careful here: a self-giving love does not ask people to sacrifice themselves in harmful relationships, and it does not tell us to let people trample us. Jesus gave his life for us to save people from sin, not so that sin could continue. True self-giving brings life to people and does not bring them harm.

Today, we can start with small things: give up our convenience, and give away our time.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he laid down his life for his friends, giving himself out of freedom and love. The Bible is my standard: greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us strength and wisdom to give ourselves. Self-giving is for Jesus and for others, not for myself, but it does not mean letting people harm me.
think: How does John 15:13 describe the greatest love?
Lately, have I been willing to set aside my own convenience for someone?
Is my “sacrifice” out of the freedom of love, or out of fear or compulsion?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you laid down your life for me, and I am not worthy. Make me willing to set aside my own convenience for others, and help me discern what is self-giving out of love and what is forced sacrifice. Holy Spirit, give me wisdom and courage, so that in love I also have boundaries. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, for a friend or family member, give up a little convenience on your own initiative: give up a seat, bring breakfast, walk with them for a stretch. And pray in your heart: Lord, this is for you.
lessons.quick: Self-giving comes from the freedom of love, not from forced sacrifice.
text: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.

lessons.title: Love the Brothers, Honor One Another
lessons.hear:
When Xiaoxin and her boyfriend argued, he said, “Why are you so stupid?” After saying it, he didn’t apologize, and he said he was only joking. Xiaoxin said nothing, but she was deeply hurt.

Paul says, “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another.” (Rom 12:10) Love is not only affectionate; it is also respectful. Affection is warmth, respect is honor, and neither can be missing.

A common mistake in dating is that, because we’re familiar, we lose our manners; because we’re close, we speak carelessly. But the closer someone is, the more they deserve to be respected.

“Prefer one another” is not fighting to be the one who loses out; it is honoring one another in how we speak, decide, and carry ourselves.

If someone speaks to you in a way that puts you down, mocks you, or humiliates you, and calls it “joking,” that is not a joke. That is harm. You deserve to be respected.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he respected every person, even children, women, and those looked down on. The Bible is my standard: in love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us see that people are made in God’s image. A person living for self speaks carelessly; a selfless person respects people as those God has made.
think: How does Rom 12:10 ask us to treat brothers and sisters?
Have I lost respect in the way I speak because I’ve become familiar with someone?
How can I treat a close person again today with honoring words?
lessons.speak: Lord, you made people in your image, and every person deserves to be respected. Forgive me for the times I spoke carelessly, and help me treat everyone with both affection and honor. Holy Spirit, guard my mouth so that my words build people up. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, use respectful words with someone close to you: say “please,” “thank you,” and “I’m sorry” once each, and notice whether any joke has hurt someone.
lessons.quick: Affection and honor are both essential; you deserve to be respected.
text: In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,

lessons.title: Love Is from God
lessons.hear:
Cheng felt that loving God was abstract. He said, “I can’t see God, so how do I love him?”

John says, “Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.” (1 John 4:11) Then he says that no one has seen God, but if we love one another, God remains in us (1 John 4:12).

Loving God is not only a feeling during devotions; it is also seen in the actions of loving people. When we love one another, we become a window through which others see God.

This is a great honor: the people we love can feel God’s love through us. It is also a great responsibility: how well we love will affect how others come to know God.

The source of love is God. We are not the source of love, but its channel.

Later, while visiting elderly people every week, Cheng discovered that God had been there all along.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the image of the invisible God, revealing the Father’s love. The Bible is my standard: if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets God’s love be seen by others through us. A person living for self thinks he is the source of love; a selfless person is a channel of God’s love.
think: What does 1 John 4:11 say is the reason we should love one another?
In my love, do others see me, or God?
Today, how can I become a channel of God’s love?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for loving me first. Make me a channel of your love, so that others see your love in me. Holy Spirit, help me set down my own pride and let only your love flow through me. The glory is yours. And help me rely on you every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one thing for someone who needs care, and say in your heart: this is a sign of God’s love for you. Don’t look for anything in return, and don’t look for praise.
lessons.quick: The source of love is God; we are the channels of his love.
text: Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

lessons.title: Love One Another Fervently from the Heart
lessons.hear:
This week, we walked through the new commandment in the Gospel of John: love one another as Jesus loved us; self-giving is the highest expression of love; love needs both affection and respect; and love is from God.

Peter says, “Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit in sincere brotherly affection, love one another from the heart fervently.” (1 Pet 1:22) The order of love is: obey the truth, purify yourself, love without pretense, and then love fervently.

Love is not something we produce by effort and pretend; it flows out naturally from a heart of truth and purity.

Don’t be discouraged; we fall short in many ways in love. God doesn’t look at how much we have loved, but at whether we are willing to return to his love and let him change us.

Humility overcomes pride, and love will become our life.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved us to the end, without pretense. The Bible is my standard: love one another from the heart fervently. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he purifies our hearts so that we love without pretense. This week’s review: where is the self in me? How did God support me? Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: What does 1 Pet 1:22 say is the precondition for loving the brothers?
This week, where did I see self in me? How did God support me in it?
In which relationship will I love fervently from the heart?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for teaching me what love is this week. Purify my heart so that I love without pretense. Holy Spirit, renew me every day so that in every relationship I can show Christ’s love. All the glory is yours. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write: the self I saw this week; God’s support; and one person I will love from the heart. Today, begin with a sincere message or a visit.
lessons.quick: Love fervently from the heart: love becomes our life.
text: Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit in sincere brotherly affection, love one another from the heart fervently,

weeks.title: Joy
weeks.theme: The root of joy is in the Lord, not in how fast the other person responds.
group: Read Phil 4:4. What is the difference between joy and happiness?
What does your joy often depend on? What does it look like to depend on the Lord?
In which difficulty this week can you say, “Even so, I will still rejoice”?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday, share with a companion one thing you are thankful for, and pray for one difficulty each of you is facing. Pass on “joy depends on the Lord” to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, hold a “thanksgiving gathering” with friends or your group: each person shares three things God has done, sings a hymn together, and prays for anyone who is going through a hard time. This doesn’t require that you be dating anyone; it is preparation for everyone.

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqing had been having a rough time with both her exams and her love life. A friend urged her, “You need to rejoice!” But in her heart she thought: how can I possibly rejoice?

Paul says, “Rejoice in the Lord always!” (Phil 4:4) Notice that this does not say “make yourself rejoice,” but “in the Lord.” Joy does not depend on moods or on circumstances; it depends on our relationship with the Lord.

This sentence was written while Paul was locked in prison. His circumstances were not good, yet his joy had a root.

Joy is different from happiness: happiness depends on circumstances, while joy depends on the Lord. Nor does this ask us to suppress sadness: we can cry honestly and, at the same time, have joy in the Lord.

Joy in dating isn’t given by the other person either. When you have someone, your joy doesn’t come from that person; when you don’t have someone, your joy doesn’t become any less.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: even before his suffering, he still had the joy the Father gave him. The Bible is my standard: rejoice in the Lord always. The Holy Spirit is my guide: joy is fruit the Spirit bears. The joy of self depends on circumstances and people; the joy of selflessness depends on the Lord. When Jesus is King, joy has a firm root.
think: What does Phil 4:4 say is the source of joy?
Does my joy right now depend on circumstances, on people, or on the Lord?
Today, how can I still give thanks to God in the midst of a difficulty?
lessons.speak: Lord, my moods often rise and fall. Let my joy depend not on circumstances or on anyone else, but on you. Holy Spirit, bear the fruit of joy in me, so that in good times and bad I can give thanks to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three things you are thankful for and read them aloud to God, inviting him to rejoice with you. If you are very sad today, first be honest with God, and then add one thing to thank him for.
lessons.quick: Joy depends on the Lord, not on circumstances; when you are sad, you can be honest too.
text: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

lessons.title: The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength
lessons.hear:
Kai felt tense every day, always struggling between “things I have to do” and “things I can’t do.” He said, “I have no strength left.”

Nehemiah said to the people, “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” (Neh 8:10) At that time, the people had heard the book of the law and wept. Nehemiah and Ezra said: today is a holy day, so don’t be grieved; go, eat and drink, and share.

God’s joy is our strength. It is not gained through our effort, but because he delights in us and his grace is enough.

Many people treat their spiritual life like a performance record, as if they need to work harder for more. But God wants us first to find strength in his joy, and then to serve and love people.

It is the same in dating: first be filled in the Lord, and then you will have enough love to give people, instead of taking from others.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he lived and served in the Father’s delight. The Bible is my standard: the joy of the LORD is your strength. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he brings us into God’s joy. A person living for self holds himself up by his own effort; a selfless person gains strength from God’s joy.
think: According to Neh 8:10, where does our strength come from?
Is my present exhaustion because I have been holding myself up on my own for too long?
Today, how can I be still before God and receive his joy?
lessons.speak: Father, I am already so tired. Help me lay down my own effort and enter your joy. Let your joy be my strength, so that I no longer hold myself up on my own but rely on you. Holy Spirit, renew my heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, set aside fifteen minutes, turn off your phone, and say to God in the quiet: I am resting; let your joy be my strength. Listen to a hymn or read a psalm.
lessons.quick: God’s joy is our strength, not our effort.
text: Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”

lessons.title: His Joy Remains in You
lessons.hear:
Mei often felt that her joy was “borrowed”: she was happy when someone praised her and down when no one noticed her. She said, “How can I have a joy that can’t be shaken?”

Jesus said, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11) In Jesus’ words is his own joy, which he wants to put in our hearts.

This is the key: the joy he gives is “my joy,” the joy of being with the Father, a joy that cannot be shaken.

How do we receive it? Through the words that came before: abiding in his love and keeping his commandments. Joy is the natural result of abiding in him.

In dating, this is a great freedom: I don’t need the other person to complete my joy, because I have already received it from Jesus.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he has perfect joy and wants to give it to us. The Bible is my standard: that my joy may remain in you. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he puts Jesus’ joy into our hearts. A person living for self begs people for joy; a selfless person receives joy from Jesus.
think: What does John 15:11 say Jesus wants to put in our hearts?
Who do I often need to complete my joy?
Today, how can I abide in Jesus’ love and receive his joy?
lessons.speak: Jesus, thank you for being willing to give me your joy. Help me not to ask people for joy but to receive it from you. Holy Spirit, let your joy grow in my heart, so that I am satisfied and can share joy with others. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, read John 15:1–11, spend two quiet minutes inviting Jesus’ joy into your heart, and then record the greatest joy of your day in your journal.
lessons.quick: Jesus’ joy can remain in our hearts, and it is full.
text: I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.

lessons.title: That You May Abound in Hope
lessons.hear:
Xiaoru was stuck in a cycle of waiting and disappointment: no news in her love life, and work wasn’t going well either. She said, “I really can’t see any hope.”

Paul says, “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.” (Rom 15:13) This verse is a blessing, and also a prayer. Hope is given by God; we can’t force it.

Notice the key phrases: “in believing” means entrusting your heart to God, and “in the power of the Holy Spirit” means not relying on your own strength.

Hope does not mean saying “everything will surely get better.” It means knowing that whatever the outcome, God is with me, he is in control, and he is good.

Hope in dating comes from here too: our ultimate hope is not a certain person, but God himself.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: for the joy that was set before him, he endured the cross. The Bible is my standard: may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes us abound in hope. A person living for self places hope in a certain outcome; a selfless person places hope in God.
think: According to Rom 15:13, who gives hope, and by what power?
What am I placing my hope in right now?
Today, how can I hand one disappointment over to the God of hope?
lessons.speak: God of hope, thank you for being my hope. Fill my heart with joy and peace, so that I no longer place my hope in people and outcomes. Holy Spirit, let your power be in me so that I abound in hope, and make me a source of hope for others. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down your biggest disappointment right now, pray and hand it over to God, and then write one Bible verse as the hope for that disappointment and put it where you will often see it.
lessons.quick: Hope is a gift from God; it depends not on outcomes but on God himself.
text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.

lessons.title: Even So, I Will Still Rejoice
lessons.hear:
This week, we walked through the lessons on joy: joy depends on the Lord, God’s joy is our strength, Jesus gives us his joy, and God gives hope. On the last day, we read a very powerful verse.

Habakkuk says, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD,” and be joyful in the God of his salvation. (Hab 3:18) Before that, he says the fig tree doesn’t flourish, the vines bear no fruit, and the fields produce no food. In other words: everything I depend on is gone. Yet he still chooses to rejoice.

“Even so, I will still rejoice” is a choice of faith: not seeing that everything is good, but seeing that God is good.

Perhaps your love life, your work, or your health is in winter right now. You don’t need to pretend nothing is wrong, but you can choose: I will still stay in him.

Don’t be discouraged. Joy is a lifelong practice; humility overcomes pride, and faith overcomes what the eye can see.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: even in his anguish in Gethsemane, he still said, not my will, but yours. The Bible is my standard: yet I will rejoice in the LORD, and be joyful in the God of my salvation. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets us have joy even in suffering. This week’s review: where is the self in me? How did God support me? Let Jesus be King, and give all the glory to God.
think: What does the “yet” in Hab 3:18 show?
This week, where did I see self in me? How did God support me in it?
What is my “winter” right now? How can I choose God in the midst of it?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for being my joy and my strength. In my winter, help me still choose you. Holy Spirit, let me find joy not through circumstances but through you. All the glory is yours. And help me choose to trust you every day. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write: the self I saw this week; God’s support; and what my “even so” is right now. Today, offer this choice to God in a prayer or a hymn.
lessons.quick: Even so, I will still rejoice, because God is good.
text: For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!

weeks.keyText: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”

weeks.title: Peace
weeks.theme: Christ’s peace does not depend on the other person’s response; it means letting him rule in my heart.
group: In John 14:27, how is the peace Jesus gives different from the peace the world gives?
In relationships, what is most likely to rob you of your peace? How do you usually react?
This week, which thing you can’t let go of do you want to hand over to the rule of Christ’s peace?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a companion. Each of you share one thing that has recently left you without peace, and then pray for each other with one sentence: “May the peace of Christ rule in your heart.” When you get home, copy Col 3:15 onto a sticky note.
weeks.weekend: Set aside a “half-day of peace” this weekend: turn off notifications, take a one-hour walk, and tell God, one by one, the people and matters you can’t let go of. Afterward, reach out to a friend you haven’t contacted in a long time, expressing only care, with no demands.

lessons.title: Jesus Leaves Us Peace
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqi had an argument with the person she had been dating for three months, and afterward the other person didn’t reply to her messages for three days. She held her phone, refreshing it again and again, her heart racing, unable to do anything else.

Before leaving the world, Jesus said to his disciples, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you.” (John 14:27) The peace the world gives depends on circumstances improving: I can relax once the other person replies; I can feel secure once the relationship is stable. But the peace Jesus gives is a peace that can still stand in the middle of a storm.

He goes on: “Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.” (John 14:27) This is not telling us to pretend nothing is wrong, but inviting us to settle our hearts in him. Whether or not the other person replies, I am still someone God loves.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: even before the cross, he had the Father’s peace. The Bible is my standard: my peace I give to you. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he puts Christ’s peace in our hearts. For a person living for self, peace hangs on the other person’s reaction; for a selfless person, peace hangs on Christ. The 9-2-0 practice: peace comes first, and then the fruit of love can grow.
think: According to John 14:27, how is the peace Jesus gives different from what the world gives?
Whose response does my peace depend on right now?
What sentence can I use today to hand my heart back to Christ?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving me your peace. I often become restless because of the other person’s coldness or silence. Settle my heart in your love so that I am not shaken by other people’s reactions. Holy Spirit, help me to have your peace even while I wait. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you can’t resist refreshing the other person’s profile or messages, stop first, close your eyes, take three deep breaths, and say to God, “Give me your peace.” Then put your phone down for ten minutes.
lessons.quick: Jesus’ peace does not depend on the other person’s response; it can still stand in the middle of a storm.
text: Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.

lessons.title: Live at Peace with Everyone, as Far as You Can
lessons.hear:
Zhi and a former coworker had a falling out, and every time they met at a gathering, both pretended not to see each other. He thought: I’ve been perfectly polite; it’s the other person’s problem.

Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” (Rom 12:18) This sentence carries two reminders. First, “as much as it is up to you” means that peace requires us to give of ourselves proactively, not to wait for the other person to move first. Second, “if it is possible” means that peace is not one-sided; sometimes the other person is unwilling, and we don’t need to force it.

More importantly, if the other person has hurt, threatened, or controlled us, peace comes not from going back to them but from a safe distance and clear boundaries. To do our part is to do all we can on our side: not retaliating, not spreading talk, not holding grudges, and leaving the door for God to open.

This week, start with your own heart: no retaliation, no spreading talk, and no letting bitterness take root.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he often reached out to people on his own, yet he did not hand himself over to those who wanted to harm him. The Bible is my standard: if it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all people. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he tells me what I should do this time. A selfless person does his own part and hands the rest over to God.
think: What does “if it is possible” in Rom 12:18 remind me of?
With which person can I take the initiative and do my part?
In what situation is keeping a distance more in line with God’s heart than forcing a meeting?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me wisdom to know when to draw near and when to keep my distance. Help me do my part, without retaliation or grudges. If there is anyone unsafe, protect me and give me clear boundaries. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down one person you want to make peace with, and one small thing you can do on your side (such as a greeting, or not passing along a message). If that person has hurt you, write only how you will protect yourself.
lessons.quick: Doing my part for peace means doing what I can on my side, not forcing myself back into harm.
text: If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

lessons.title: Let Christ’s Peace Rule
lessons.hear:
Every time Zhiqing thought about the future, she began to calculate: What if he isn’t the right person? What if I choose wrong? It was as if two voices were arguing in her heart.

Paul says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.” (Col 3:15) “Rule” means to arbitrate, like the umpire in a game who makes the call. When there are many voices in the heart, we let Christ’s peace be the umpire and see which voice brings peace and which brings anxiety and confusion.

But be careful: peace is not a good mood, and it is not the absence of fear. True peace agrees with the Bible, agrees with trusted witnesses, and agrees with safety. If a decision requires you to go against the Bible, suppress your conscience, or leaves you more isolated, that is not Christ’s peace.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in Gethsemane, he still handed his will over to the Father. The Bible is my standard: let Christ’s peace rule in your hearts. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he confirms with peace the direction that fits God’s will. Letting Jesus be King means letting his peace be the umpire, and not letting fear and impulse be king.
think: What does Col 3:15 say Christ’s peace should do in our hearts?
