What is the loudest thing in my heart right now: anxiety, impulse, or Christ’s peace?
Do I have someone with whom I can test my peace?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, let your peace rule in my heart. When there are many voices in my heart, help me discern which one is yours. Please also give me trustworthy companions to seek your will with me. I will keep a thankful heart. Amen.
lessons.do: Take one thing you are struggling with and write it in two columns: “Voices that make me anxious” and “The voice of the Bible and peace.” Then read it to a trusted companion and ask for his or her view.
lessons.quick: Let Christ’s peace be the umpire: see which voice fits the Bible and also brings peace.
text: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

lessons.title: Don’t Let the Sun Go Down on Your Anger
lessons.hear:
In the group chat, Xiaozhe was stung by a joke from the person he was dating. He said nothing at the time but kept it in his heart. Three days later, he exploded over another small matter and brought up a pile of old grievances. Both of them were shocked.

Paul says, “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil.” (Eph 4:26–27) The Bible does not say “you must not be angry.” Anger is a human feeling, and it often reminds us that something has been touched. But we have to deal with it: not let it stay overnight, and not keep it bottled up to ferment.

Holding on to anger is like putting a hot coal in your pocket; sooner or later it burns you. “Sundown” reminds us to deal with it that same day, in God’s presence: first say it to God, then choose an appropriate time and way to explain it to the other person, honestly and without blame.

If the other person might threaten or hurt you because of it, protect yourself first and ask a trusted person to be with you.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he felt righteous anger in the temple, yet he did not sin and did not retaliate. The Bible is my standard: be angry, and don’t sin; don’t let the sun go down on your anger. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets me keep self-control even in anger. A person living for self uses anger as a weapon; a selfless person hands anger over to God and then speaks the truth in love.
think: According to Eph 4:26–27, what two things should we not do when we are angry?
Have I recently held on to anger overnight? What has it grown into in my heart?
Today, how can I honestly hand over this anger?
lessons.speak: Lord, sometimes I get angry and don’t know what to do. First accept my anger, and then teach me to say it honestly and gently. Don’t let me hold on to anger until sundown, and don’t let the devil gain a foothold in my heart. Holy Spirit, give me self-control. Amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, spend five minutes telling God the anger in your heart, and then write one blame-free “I” sentence, for example: “When…, I felt…, and I need….”
lessons.quick: Don’t keep anger overnight: first tell God, then speak the truth in love.
text: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
and don’t give place to the devil.

lessons.title: Pray About Everything, and God’s Peace Will Guard You
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: Jesus leaves us his peace (John 14:27); live at peace with everyone as far as you can (Rom 12:18); let Christ’s peace rule (Col 3:15); don’t keep anger overnight (Eph 4:26–27).

Paul says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Phil 4:6–7) Prayer is not about thinking things through more clearly; it is about exchanging the burdens in our hearts for God’s peace.

Notice that “guard” is like a sentry standing at the door of the heart. Our responsibility is to tell God our anxieties; God’s responsibility is to guard our hearts with his peace.

This week, where did I see self in me? Was it being anxious for the other person’s response, or being unwilling to let go of anger? And how did God support me?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, giving us his peace; the Bible is my standard, letting Christ’s peace rule; the Holy Spirit is my guide, guarding our hearts with peace. Let people be people, and let God be God: we cannot control the other person, but we can hand our anxieties over to God. The glory is his.
think: This week, where did I see self in me?
According to Phil 4:6–7, what do we exchange our anxieties for? How does God guard our hearts?
Which anxiety will I hand over to God every day next week?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for hearing my prayer. I hand you my anxieties, my expectations, and my fears. With a peace that surpasses understanding, guard my heart and my thoughts. May I live out Christ’s peace in my relationships. All the glory is yours. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write: the one thing that took away my peace most this week; how I prayed to God about it; and how God supported me. Then choose someone you want to make peace with and pray for him or her for one minute.
lessons.quick: Tell God your anxieties, and his peace will guard my heart.
text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

weeks.keyText: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

weeks.title: Patience
weeks.theme: Patience is not putting up with harm; it is waiting steadily for God’s timing, with hope.
group: In James 5:7–8, what is special about the way the farmer waits?
In which part of your love life or daily life is waiting hardest for you?
This week, how do you want to hold on to hope while you wait?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner and share one thing you are waiting for, then pray for each other: “Lord, strengthen your heart.” Also send an encouraging word to a friend who is waiting.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, plant a small pot of something or care for anything that takes time (baking bread or practicing an instrument works too). Notice one small change each day, and invite a friend to share what they observe, so you can learn the lesson of waiting together.

lessons.title: The Waiting Farmer
lessons.hear:
Lan had been single for many years, and her friends were getting married one by one. At every gathering, someone asked, “Why don’t you have someone yet?” She smiled and said it would be soon, but at home she couldn’t help feeling sad.

James says, “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.” (Jas 5:7–8) A farmer can’t make a seed sprout at once, but he isn’t idle: he turns the soil, waters, weeds, and keeps watch. Patience means doing what we should do while entrusting the growth to God.

Notice that this is about waiting for the Lord, not waiting for a person. Our hope is in the Lord, not in a partner; and it is not telling anyone to put up with harm. Patience is strengthening our heart, not suppressing it.

The days of waiting are the days when God is working within us.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he waited thirty years before beginning his public ministry, obeying the Father’s timing at every step. The Bible is my standard: the farmer waits patiently, and you also be patient; establish your hearts. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he produces the fruit of patience. A life of self is hurried to control time; a life of selflessness hands time over to God.
think: According to James 5:7–8, what does the farmer wait for patiently?
What am I most anxious to change right now? What worry in my heart does my hurry reveal?
What is one “small thing a farmer would do” that I can do today?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often wait impatiently, and I often feel lonely. Strengthen my heart, so that like a farmer I do my part while entrusting the growth to you. Let my hope be in you, not in another person. Amen.
lessons.do: Choose one thing you are waiting for, and today do just one “small thing a farmer would do,” such as praying, preparing, tidying up, or studying. When you finish, write one sentence of thanks in your journal.
lessons.quick: Patience is doing what we should while handing the timing to God.
text: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

lessons.title: If We Hope, We Wait with Patience
lessons.hear:
After his breakup, Kai often told his friends, “I’ve let it go.” But every night he still looked at his ex’s social media page, and each time it hurt more.

Paul says, “But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience.” (Rom 8:25) Hope is being sure of what we have not yet seen. Patience is choosing to keep believing in the days when we still can’t see it.

The passage this verse sits in speaks of creation groaning as it waits for the freedom of glory. Our hope is ultimately Christ’s return and God making all things new, not just a wish close at hand. The greater the foundation of our hope, the steadier our waiting heart.

So healing is not forcing ourselves to get better fast. It is giving hope a place to stand through small daily choices: checking their page one less time, praying one more time, walking with one more friend.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: for the joy set before him, he endured the cross. The Bible is my standard: if we hope for what we don’t see, we wait for it with patience. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps us in our weakness. A selfless person places hope in eternity, not in a single outcome.
think: According to Romans 8:25, what is the foundation for waiting with patience?
Where is my hope placed right now? In a person, or in God?
What is one small choice I can make today that gives hope a place to stand?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you are my hope that never fails. Sometimes I can’t see the road ahead, and my heart is tired. Build my hope on you, give me patience, and help me wait one day at a time. Holy Spirit, hold me up when I am weak. Amen.
lessons.do: Today do one small thing that helps you heal: tell a trusted friend what you are feeling, or write down in your journal three pieces of evidence that God is still watching over you.
lessons.quick: The more our hope rests on God, the steadier our waiting heart.
text: But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience.

lessons.title: Bearing with One Another in Love
lessons.hear:
Xiaowei’s boyfriend was often late. The first time, she said it was fine; the tenth time, she said he didn’t respect her. He said he was trying to change, but work was just too busy.

Paul says, “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love.” (Eph 4:2) To “bear with” is to put up with one another in our imperfection. Everyone has weaknesses; dating is not about finding someone with no flaws, but someone willing to grow with you.

But bearing with has its limits. Inconvenience, different habits, and personality differences are things we can bear with; control, humiliation, deception, and violence must not be covered up with the word “tolerance.” The first is carried by loving patience; the second calls for boundaries and help.

A way to tell the difference is to ask: Is this a weakness, or is it harm? Is the other person willing to face it?

Love bears with others while staying honest; it is gentle while holding the bottom line.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he put up with his disciples’ slowness, yet he also spoke plainly. The Bible is my standard: bear with one another in love. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us humility, gentleness, and patience. A selfless person can bear with others’ weaknesses and also has the courage to protect themselves from harm. May we live out the likeness of Christ in our relationships.
think: According to Ephesians 4:2, in what spirit do we bear with one another?
Is what I am putting up with right now the other person’s weakness, or harm? How do I tell?
Is there something I need to say gently out loud?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for bearing with my weaknesses. Teach me to bear with others’ imperfections in love, and give me wisdom to tell what is weakness and what is harm. If there is harm, give me courage to seek help. Let my words and actions carry your gentleness. Amen.
lessons.do: List one thing you are bearing with, and ask yourself: Is this a weakness or harm? If it is a weakness, write down one gentle request; if it is harm, tell a trusted person today.
lessons.quick: Bear with weakness, but don’t excuse harm; if in doubt, talk to someone you trust.
text: with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,

lessons.title: Imitate Those Who Inherit the Promises
lessons.hear:
Cheng practiced praying every day, but after a month he began to doubt: Is this doing any good? He wanted to quit, because nothing had changed.

Hebrews says, “that you won’t be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises.” (Heb 6:12) Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac; Joseph went from being sold to becoming prime minister over thirteen years. They didn’t give up because the wait was long; in the waiting, they learned to trust.

“Not sluggish” doesn’t mean being tense and straining; it means keeping on in small things: daily prayer, weekly fellowship, every honest conversation. Faith and perseverance are like two feet, walking together toward the promise.

The promise here is what God has said, not our own expectation of a particular outcome. What we imitate is the way these people walked with God.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the author and perfecter of faith. The Bible is my standard: don’t be sluggish, but imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and perseverance. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me keep going in ordinary days. It is not my own effort, but the grace of Christ. One step at a time, by your grace.
think: According to Hebrews 6:12, what kind of people are we to imitate?
Which spiritual habit am I tempted to give up on because I can’t see results?
How can I keep going one more day today?
lessons.speak: Lord, sometimes I feel I am trying hard but see no results. Keep me from being sluggish, and help me keep walking with you in faith and perseverance. Remind me that your promises are true and that you are faithful. Make my heart strong in you, renewed every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Choose a spiritual habit you are about to give up on (prayer, Bible reading, fellowship), do it once more today, and then text a partner: “Thank you for sticking with me.”
lessons.quick: Not being sluggish means keeping on one more day in small things.
text: that you won’t be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises.

lessons.title: I Waited Patiently for the Lord
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: the farmer’s waiting (Jas 5:7–8); hoping for what we don’t see (Rom 8:25); bearing with one another in love (Eph 4:2); imitating those who inherit the promises (Heb 6:12).

David says, “I waited patiently for the LORD. He turned to me, and heard my cry.” (Ps 40:1) The result of waiting is not always the answer we want, but it is always this: God hears. This is the greatest comfort in all waiting.

The psalmist goes on to say that God lifted him out of the pit and set his feet on a rock. Waiting is not wasted time; it is God working within us.

This week, where did I see my own self-centeredness? Was it impatience, complaining, or wanting to control? How did God hold me up as I waited?

You don’t have to wait alone. Say your cry out loud, and let your partner pray with you; this itself is God’s grace.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, waiting patiently for the Father’s timing; the Bible is my standard, with the farmer’s patience and the waiting of hope; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving the fruit of patience. Let Jesus be King, and we hand our time over to him; all glory to God. May we come to know him more as we wait.
think: This week, where did I see my own self?
According to Psalm 40:1, what did God do for the one who waited patiently?
In what matter next week will I keep trusting God’s timing?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for hearing my cry. I admit I am often impatient and want to control things myself. Set my feet on the rock, and let me know you more as I wait. May all glory be to you. As I wait, help me know you more and trust you more. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: the hardest thing to wait for this week; how I responded; how God heard and held me up. Then pray for a friend who is also waiting, and send him an encouraging word.
lessons.quick: The greatest comfort in waiting: God hears.
text: I waited patiently for the LORD. He turned to me, and heard my cry.

weeks.keyText: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

weeks.title: Kindness
weeks.theme: Kindness is goodwill that takes the first step; forgiveness can be given first, but trust depends on genuine repentance.
group: According to Eph 4:32, why should we forgive one another?
Who lately needs your kindness, or your forgiveness?
This week, what small action will you use to show kindness to one person?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, say a specific word of thanks or encouragement to a brother or sister you don’t know well, then send the word “kindness” to a friend with your blessing.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, choose someone you can help (an elder, a neighbor, or a friend) and do one practical small thing for them, such as buying breakfast, walking with them for a while, or helping with an errand. Expect nothing in return, and don’t tell anyone else.

lessons.title: Be Kind and Forgive One Another
lessons.hear:
After the breakup, Xin kept holding resentment toward her ex. A friend urged her, “You should forgive.” But inside she thought, “If I forgive, does that mean he did nothing wrong? Do I have to go back to him?”

Paul says, “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Eph 4:32) God’s forgiveness is the basis for our forgiving others. But forgiving does not mean saying “it’s no big deal,” and it does not mean returning to the old relationship.

Forgiveness is handing over to God the right to collect the debt, so that resentment no longer binds us; trust, however, requires genuine repentance and long-term change from the other person. Forgiveness can be given first, by one side alone, but trust cannot.

If you have been hurt, your pain is real, and you don’t need to rush to say “I have forgiven.” You can take it one step at a time, walking with God and with trusted companions.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he prayed for his enemies, yet he never demanded that the victim return to the one who hurt them. The Bible is my standard: be kind, be tender hearted, forgive each other. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he sets me free from resentment. A life of self clings to the hurt; a life of selflessness hands the hurt to God.
think: According to Eph 4:32, what is the basis for our forgiving others?
Have I ever confused forgiving with going back into harm?
What weight of resentment am I willing to hand over to God today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for forgiving me in Christ. There is a wound in my heart; please heal it. Help me hand over to you the right to collect the debt, and give me wisdom to know when to keep my distance. Protect me, and give me peace. Amen.
lessons.do: On a piece of paper, write the name or event that hurt you, and say to God, “I hand this to you.” When you finish, tear it up or put it away. If the harm involves violence or threats, please contact a professional (see “I Need Help”).
lessons.quick: Forgiveness is handing over the right to collect the debt; trust depends on genuine repentance.
text: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Compassion, Kindness, Humility
lessons.hear:
At a small group, Hao noticed a new sister sitting in the corner, and no one went over to greet her. He thought, “Maybe someone will,” and looked down at his phone. When it ended, she was the first to leave.

Paul says, “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance.” (Col 3:12) Notice that Paul first says we are “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved,” and only then says “Put on.” We are loved first, and then we learn to love.

Like getting dressed, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience are new clothes to put on every day. When we wear them, we naturally notice the person in the corner among the crowd, and we walk over.

Kindness doesn’t need a romance to begin. Single people can show kindness to neighbors, coworkers, and family; those who are dating shouldn’t be good to only one person while cold to everyone else.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he always saw the people others overlooked. The Bible is my standard: as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, and humility. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds us to put on the new clothes each day. A selfless person’s eyes don’t look only at themselves, but also see the people nearby.
think: According to Col 3:12, who are we? So what are we to put on?
Have I overlooked someone nearby who needed kindness lately?
Whom can I take the initiative to approach today, and what can I say?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for calling me one you love. Help me put on compassion, kindness, and humility every day, not only when I want to be loved, but also to see those in need among the crowd. Holy Spirit, give me courage to go to them first. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, go to someone who is easily overlooked (a new friend, an elder, or a coworker) and say something specific, such as “Thank you for today…,” or invite them to eat together.
lessons.quick: First know you are loved, then love the person in front of you.
text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;

lessons.title: Do to Others What You Would Have Them Do to You
lessons.hear:
In dating, Xiaolian always wanted her partner to remember her birthday and ask her on his own how her day was. She often said, “Why doesn’t he understand me at all?” Then one day a friend asked her, “Have you treated him that way?” She was stunned.

Jesus says, “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.” (Luke 6:31) These words are like a mirror: whatever I expect from others, I should first check whether I treat others that way.

This is not a trade, “I’m good to you, so you must be good to me.” It is goodwill that takes the first step: I begin, without waiting for the other. Nor does it mean pleasing people or suppressing our own needs; it means looking at others with empathy: I want to be respected, so I respect people; I want to be listened to, so I am willing to listen.

This is a golden rule for walking through all of life, and it is especially precious in dating.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he loved us first, not waiting for us to love him first. The Bible is my standard: as you would like people to do to you, do the same to them. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives us empathy. A life of self demands from others first; a life of selflessness gives first, letting God be God and people be people.
think: According to Luke 6:31, what standard do we use in treating others?
Is there something I expect from others that I don’t do myself?
What kind of treatment that I hope to receive can I give first today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often expect others to understand me, but forget to understand them first. Help me give respect, listening, and kindness first, instead of only waiting for others to give them to me. Put your love in my heart, so that I may be a blessing to others. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down three ways you hope others would treat you (such as respect, listening, thanks). Today pick one, and do it first for someone near you.
lessons.quick: Give first the treatment you hope to receive.
text: “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.

lessons.title: Never Let Kindness and Truth Leave You
lessons.hear:
In dating, An often said things that weren’t quite true to keep his partner from getting angry: “It’s nothing,” “Anything is fine with me,” “I like it a lot.” After a while, his partner assumed everything was fine with him, while he grew more and more tired.

Proverbs says, “Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.” (Prov 3:3) Kindness and truth are a pair: kindness without truth turns into people-pleasing; truth without kindness turns into hurting people. Only together are they the love of Christ.

“Bound around the neck” is an ornament seen every day; “written on the heart” is a mark that never wears away. May our words be both true and gentle.

Concretely, it means speaking truth in a kind tone: not hiding, not exaggerating, and not blaming.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was full of grace and truth. The Bible is my standard: don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of grace. A life of self either pleases or criticizes; a selfless person in Christ has both love and truth.
think: According to Prov 3:3, what must not leave us?
Which side do I usually lean toward: only kindness, or only truth?
What can I say today that is both honest and gentle?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are full of grace and full of truth. Help me in my relationships not to please people, not to hide things, and not to hurt anyone. Write kindness and truth on the tablet of my heart, so that all my words carry your love. And help me learn every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Think of one true thing you have never said out loud, and write it down with “kindness + truth”: first affirm, then say your feelings and needs. You can practice first with a trusted partner.
lessons.quick: Kindness plus truth is the love of Christ.
text: Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

lessons.title: A Heart of Humility and Compassion
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: treating people with kindness and forgiving one another (Eph 4:32); putting on compassion, kindness, and humility (Col 3:12); giving first what we hope to receive (Luke 6:31); kindness and truth walking together (Prov 3:3).

Peter says, “not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.” (1 Pet 3:9) When we are hurt, the most natural reaction is to strike back; but in Christ, we are called to respond with blessing.

This does not mean we must stay in the harm. Blessing means not taking revenge and not cursing, and leaving judgment to God; but we can still protect ourselves and leave danger.

This week, where did I see my own self-centeredness? How did God hold me up with his kindness?

A person who blesses has God’s peace in their heart.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, who did not answer back when reviled; the Bible is my standard, not repaying evil for evil, but blessing; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving me the fruit of kindness. Let Jesus be King, and we do not repay evil for evil; glory to God. Let people be people and God be God: judgment is God’s business, and blessing is ours.
think: This week, where did I see my own self?
According to 1 Pet 3:9, how should we respond when we are reviled?
Whom can I bless next week, and how will I protect myself?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for your kindness that has come to me. I admit I often want to strike back and take revenge. Help me not to repay evil for evil, but to bless. Protect me too, so that I rest securely in your kindness and become a blessing to others. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: where I saw my own self this week; how God held me up. Then, for someone who hurt you, pray a blessing without bitterness (you don’t need to contact them).
lessons.quick: Blessing doesn’t mean staying in the harm; it means not taking revenge and handing it to God.
text: Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous,
not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.

weeks.keyText: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

weeks.title: Goodness
weeks.theme: Goodness is sincerely seeking another’s good; it is neither people-pleasing nor being used.
group: According to Rom 15:2, what is the purpose of doing good?
What is the difference between goodness and people-pleasing? When did you last do a “good deed” out of people-pleasing?
For whom do you want to do something this week that truly benefits them?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, ask a partner, “How can I help you this week?” Then listen carefully to the end, and set aside one hour to carry out the answer.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, arrange a time of “silent service”: at church, in the community, or at home, find a job no one notices (cleaning, tidying, delivering a meal), and do it without taking photos or sharing, telling only God.

lessons.title: Let Each of Us Please His Neighbor
lessons.hear:
Zhen was very good at caring for people, and when a friend came to her with a need, she never refused. But after people left she often felt very tired, even a little angry: “I’m so good to everyone, so why does no one care about me?”

Paul says, “Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.” (Rom 15:2) Notice that the purpose is “for that which is good, to be building him up,” not making someone happy for a moment, and certainly not earning thanks in return. A people-pleaser watches people’s faces; a good person watches people’s good.

Sometimes goodness needs to say no. To a friend who loves gambling, saying “I won’t lend you money” may upset him in the moment, but it is truly good for him. Goodness also includes caring for ourselves, because a person who has run dry cannot keep blessing others.

Loving our neighbor as ourselves means giving with self-control and drawing strength from God’s provision.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: sometimes he healed, sometimes he left the crowds to pray, and he also said no to people. The Bible is my standard: please your neighbor for that which is good, to build him up. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me the fruit of goodness, and he gives me wisdom. A life of self does good to earn a reward; a life of selflessness does good so that Christ’s love flows outward.
think: According to Rom 15:2, what is the purpose of doing good?
Is my giving often out of love, or out of fear of being disliked?
Whom can I do something truly beneficial for today, even if it means gently saying “no”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often want to please people, but I forget what they truly need. Give me wisdom to discern what is truly good for them. Give me both the strength to give and the courage to say no. I will find my strength in you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one thing that is truly good for one person. If there is something you have been reluctantly agreeing to, decline it with gentle words, and say to yourself, “I can love others, and I can also take care of myself.”
lessons.quick: Goodness looks to people’s good, not to people’s faces.
text: Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.

lessons.title: Love Your Enemies, and Do Good
lessons.hear:
Xiaowei was publicly criticized by his ex on social media, and he was deeply hurt. A friend said, “You have to love your enemies!” He was confused inside: Does loving my enemy mean I should be in touch with him again, or keep being hurt by him?

Jesus says, “But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.” (Luke 6:35) Loving enemies means not taking revenge, not cursing, being willing to pray for their good, and doing good to them within what is possible.

It does not tell us to go back to a dangerous person, nor to pretend we were not hurt. Jesus himself also left those who wanted to harm him. Loving an enemy can mean praying for him from a safe distance; and when necessary, through appropriate channels, seeking help and defending justice.

Because God is kind toward the unthankful and evil, we too are people who have received this kindness.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: on the cross he prayed for those who nailed him there. The Bible is my standard: love your enemies, and do good to them. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he keeps us from being ruled by bitterness. A life of self repays evil with evil; a life of selflessness hands judgment to God and also seeks justice. We too are people who have received grace.
think: According to Luke 6:35, why should we love our enemies?
What do I feel right now toward the person who hurt me?
As long as it is safe, how can I pray for his good?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for being kind to me, an unthankful person. There is someone in my heart who hurt me; please heal my wound, and have mercy on him too. Protect me and give me wisdom, so that I do not take revenge and do not force myself back into danger. Amen.
lessons.do: As long as it is safe, pray for one minute for someone who hurt you, asking only that God show them grace and guard your heart. If you are still in a situation of being hurt, please first contact a trusted person or professional help.
lessons.quick: Loving enemies is not going back into harm; it is not taking revenge and handing it to God.
text: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.

lessons.title: Overcome Evil with Good
lessons.hear:
En found out that a friend had been gossiping about him behind his back. He was furious and planned to talk about that person in the group chat too. Halfway through typing, he stopped, because he remembered a verse.

Paul says, “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Rom 12:21) This has two layers: first, don’t be swayed by evil and become like the other person; second, use good to overcome evil.

Notice in particular that being “overcome by evil” is not only being knocked down, but also becoming evil ourselves in order to take revenge. When we repay evil with evil, evil wins; when we choose not to retaliate, even if it is only a word left unsaid, at that moment we have overcome evil.

Overcoming evil with good also includes opposing injustice in good ways: gathering evidence, reporting, and seeking help are all good. It is not passive silence.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he overcame death and sin with love and truth. The Bible is my standard: don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me self-control even when evil attacks me. A life of self goes along with evil; a selfless person overcomes through Christ. A selfless person does not rely on their own strength.
think: According to Rom 12:21, what must we not do? What must we do instead?
What lately made me want to repay evil with evil?
What good action can I use today to overcome that evil thought?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for overcoming evil with love. When I want revenge, make me stop. Keep me from being overcome by evil, and let me overcome evil with good. Holy Spirit, give me wisdom and courage, and give me peace. Give me strength and wisdom. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you want to answer someone with negative words, pause for ten seconds, write down that sentence, then tear it up, and instead write one honest sentence with no attack in it, or choose not to reply. If you face illegal acts or violence, please seek professional help.
lessons.quick: Don’t repay evil with evil; overcome evil with good, and you may also seek justice.
text: Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.title: Always Pursue What Is Good, for Everyone
lessons.hear:
Yuan was a very passionate sister, kind to everyone at church, but cold to her family. She said, “In front of my family, I don’t have to pretend.”

Paul says, “See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.” (1 Thess 5:15) “To anyone” includes friends, strangers, and coworkers, and also those closest to us. “Always follow after” means this is not a passing impulse but the direction of a whole life.

If goodness is good only on the outside and bad in front of those closest to us, it is incomplete. True character is staying kind in places where no one sees, in front of the people we feel most relaxed with.

Ask yourself: Do those closest to me also feel my goodness? If not, begin today with one word and one action.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he gave the same kindness to his close disciples and to strangers. The Bible is my standard: always pursue what is good, toward everyone. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he guards our words even when we are most relaxed. A selfless person is equally good in every setting.
think: According to 1 Thess 5:15, toward whom are we to pursue what is good?
In front of whom am I most relaxed, and most likely to be unkind?
Can I say one kind word today to the person closest to me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for being kind to every person. Help me to be good even in front of those closest to me, and not to be careless just because we are familiar. Holy Spirit, guard my words even when I am relaxed. And renew me every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, say one specific word of affirmation to the person closest to you (a family member or roommate), and do one small thing for them, such as pouring water, washing dishes, or checking in.
lessons.quick: Goodness doesn’t get discounted in front of those closest to us.
text: See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.

lessons.title: Do Not Lose Heart in Doing Good
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: truly benefiting people (Rom 15:2); loving enemies (Luke 6:35); overcoming evil with good (Rom 12:21); pursuing good toward everyone (1 Thess 5:15).

Paul says, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” (Gal 6:9) Sometimes we give everything we have for people but see no response, and are even misunderstood. That is when we grow weary most easily.

“In due season” reminds us that the harvest is in God’s timing, and our responsibility is to keep sowing. Paul also says, “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.” (Gal 6:10) We don’t have to help everyone at once; we only need to seize the opportunity in front of us.

This week, where did I see my own self-centeredness? Did I want to be seen, or to be thanked? How did God hold me up through it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, who went around doing good; the Bible is my standard, do not lose heart in doing good; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving me the fruit of goodness. Let Jesus be King, and glory to him. Give thanks in everything, and give the glory to God, because all of it is grace accomplished by God.
think: This week, where did I see my own self?
According to Gal 6:9, what happens in due season if we don’t give up?
Which opportunity will I seize next week, and for whom will I do good?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for giving me opportunities to do good. Sometimes I feel tired and want to be seen. Keep me from losing heart, and let me reap in your timing. Help me seize every opportunity to do good to all. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: the most tiring thing in doing good this week; where I saw my own self; how God held me up. Then choose one opportunity to do a small good for someone in need.
lessons.quick: Do good without losing heart, and in due season you will reap.
text: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

weeks.keyText: Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.

weeks.title: Faithfulness
weeks.theme: Faithfulness starts with small things: doing what you say is the most basic shape of love.
group: According to Matt 5:37, what should our words be like?
Have I lately said something and not done it? What effect did it have on the relationship?
In which small matter this week do you want your “Yes” to be “Yes”?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner, and each share one small promise you will keep this week, then check in with each other next week. When you get home, send Matt 5:37 to a friend.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, take stock of the promises you owe others (replying to messages, returning things, plans you made), choose three, and try to finish them over the weekend, or honestly tell the other person that you need to postpone.

lessons.title: Let Your “Yes” Be “Yes”
lessons.hear:
Qian was very good at agreeing to things: “Sure, I’ll definitely be there!” “No problem, I’ll take care of it!” But when the day came, he often forgot or canceled at the last minute. His friends gradually stopped taking his words seriously.

Jesus says, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” (Matt 5:37) He wants our speech to be simple, honest, and dependable. We don’t need to swear or exaggerate, because who we are is the best guarantee.

In dating, words are even more the foundation of trust: do what you promised, and if you can’t, explain honestly; don’t casually say “I’ll love you forever,” but let the other person see your faithfulness in small things.

Faithfulness is not perfection but not hiding: if you were wrong, admit it; if you can’t do it, be frank; if you owe someone, find a way to make it up.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his word is truth, and he does what he says. The Bible is my standard: let your Yes be Yes, and your No be No. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit of truth, who makes my words dependable. A life of self wins people over with clever words; a life of selflessness earns trust through faithfulness.
think: According to Matt 5:37, what should our words be like?
When I often say “okay,” how much of it is sincere, and how much is to avoid conflict?
What action can I take today to make good on something I said?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, every word of yours is true. Help me speak honestly, Yes when it is yes and No when it is no. Forgive me for agreeing offhandedly and not following through, and help me make it up one thing at a time. Holy Spirit, make me a dependable person. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one small thing you promised but didn’t do, and finish it, or honestly say to the other person, “I didn’t do what I promised you, and here is how I’m making it up now.”
lessons.quick: Dependable words are the most basic shape of love.
text: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

lessons.title: Keeps an Oath Even When It Hurts
lessons.hear:
Qin had promised a friend that she would go with him every month to visit the elderly. Later her work got busy, and someone invited her to a more fun activity, and her heart wavered: Do I still have to keep this promise?

Psalm 15 asks: Who may dwell in God’s sanctuary? One of the answers is: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change.” (Ps 15:4) A faithful person keeps their word even when a promise becomes inconvenient, even costly.

This is not telling us to make vows lightly, but to think carefully before we make them, and once made, to do our best to keep them. If we truly can no longer keep one, we should honestly explain to the other person and ask for understanding, rather than quietly disappearing.

Note that if the original promise was made under threat or coercion, or if keeping it would hurt ourselves or others, we should seek help from trusted people rather than forcing ourselves to hold on.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his promise to the Father he obeyed even to death. The Bible is my standard: he keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me the fruit of faithfulness. A selfless person measures not by their own convenience but by faithfulness. May we be faithful to the end.
think: According to Ps 15:4, when does a faithful person still keep their word?
Is there a promise right now that I am wavering on because it is inconvenient?
How should I face it honestly?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are a faithful God who never changes your promises. Help me seek you before I make a promise, and stay true to my word when a promise becomes inconvenient. If there is something I can’t do, give me courage to explain it honestly. Amen.
lessons.do: List the three commitments you have now, and write “continue,” “adjust,” or “explain honestly” beside each one. Take action on one of them today.
lessons.quick: Faithfulness is keeping your word even when a promise is inconvenient.
text: in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;

lessons.title: Faithful in Little Things
lessons.hear:
Xiaopei said she wanted to become someone who could do great things, but she often turned in reports late and put off what she had agreed to until the last minute. One day her boss said to her, “I can’t trust you with big things.”

Jesus says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10) Faithfulness is not shown in big things; it is formed in small things. Being on time, replying to messages, returning things, telling the truth: these seemingly tiny choices determine who we are.

In a dating relationship, small things reveal character even more: How does he treat the server? How does she handle the time they agreed on? What does he do when no one is watching?

Faithfulness in small things is reverence for God: I know God is watching, and I know all of this was entrusted to me by him.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he spent thirty years in Nazareth, faithful in ordinary days. The Bible is my standard: whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me in the details. A selfless person doesn’t pick matters by size, but only asks whether it pleases the Lord.
think: According to Luke 16:10, where does faithfulness begin?
In which small thing am I most likely to be careless?
How can I be faithful for the Lord in one small thing today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you were faithful to the end in small things. Keep me from despising small things or performing only in front of people. Forgive my carelessness and procrastination, and help me do every task entrusted to me as if it were for you. And teach me faithfulness every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one small thing you often put off (answering a message, tidying your desk, returning something you borrowed), finish it right away, and say to yourself, “In small things, I am faithful for the Lord.”
lessons.quick: Faithfulness is formed in the smallest things.
text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.

lessons.title: Who Can Find a Faithful Man?
lessons.hear:
Da met someone very articulate on a dating app: “I’m very honest and very caring.” Da quickly believed it. But after spending some time together, he found that the other person’s words and actions often didn’t match, though by then he had invested a lot of feeling.

Proverbs says, “Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?” (Prov 20:6) Many people say they are good, but truly faithful people are few. We judge a person not by what they say but by their actions over a long time: their attitude toward God, their attitude toward family, how they face conflict, and how they admit mistakes.

This is also a reminder to ourselves: don’t just say “I love you”; prove it with faithfulness, day after day.

In dating, go slowly, observe more, and listen to the opinions of trusted companions. A faithful person is worth the time it takes to prove.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his love was proved by action. The Bible is my standard: who can find a faithful man? The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me discernment, and he makes me a faithful person. A selfless person doesn’t rely on self-promotion; the life of Christ is what people see. May we bear witness with our lives.
think: According to Prov 20:6, what kind of person is hard to find?
When I evaluate someone, do I value more what they say, or what they do?
Am I myself a person who “speaks through actions”?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are a faithful God. Make me a faithful person, proving it not only with words but also with actions. Give me wisdom to discern whether people’s words and actions match, and make me willing to listen to trusted companions. Amen.
lessons.do: Write down a faithful person you admire. What are three specific things they do? Say thank you to them today, and ask yourself which action you can learn from.
lessons.quick: Faithfulness is proved by actions, day after day.
text: Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?

lessons.title: Great Is Your Faithfulness
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: letting Yes be Yes (Matt 5:37); keeping an oath even when it hurts (Ps 15:4); being faithful in little things (Luke 16:10); proving faithfulness by actions (Prov 20:6).

You may have found that you are not as faithful as you imagined. At such a time, the greatest comfort is that God is faithful. Jeremiah, in the ruins of Jerusalem, says, “It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” (Lam 3:22–23)

Our faithfulness is often broken; God’s faithfulness never changes. We don’t become faithful through our own effort, but through God’s faithfulness we are renewed, day by day.

This week, where did I see my own self-centeredness? How did God’s faithfulness hold me up?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, the faithful and true witness; the Bible is my standard, let your Yes be Yes; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving me the fruit of faithfulness. Let Jesus be King, and glory to him, because all of it is God’s faithfulness. Give thanks in everything, and give the glory to Jesus, because all of it is grace accomplished by God.
think: This week, where did I see my own self?
According to Lam 3:22–23, what of God’s is new every morning?
In which matter next week will I do what I say, before God and people?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your faithfulness is so great. I often break faith, and I am often weak. Renew me every morning, so that by your faithfulness I become a dependable person. All glory to you. And help me rely on you every day, becoming newer and more dependable each day. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: one thing where I broke faith this week; how God was gracious to me in it. Then say to someone you let down, “I’m sorry, and here is how I’ll change.”
lessons.quick: God’s faithfulness is new every morning, and we are renewed through him.
text: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

weeks.keyText: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

weeks.title: Gentleness
weeks.theme: Gentleness is having strength but not using it; it can calm anger, and it can restore people.
group: In Matt 11:29, how does Jesus describe himself?
In what kind of situation is it easiest for you to speak ungently?
What gentle word do you want to use this week to respond to a situation that makes you angry?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner and take turns spending two minutes describing the most recent time you were angry; the listener says only, “Thank you for telling me.” Then pray together, asking the Lord for a gentle heart.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, practice “slowing down”: eat one meal slowly, walk a stretch slowly, and slowly listen to someone until they finish, without interrupting or defending yourself. Afterward, write down how slowing down affected your heart.

lessons.title: I Am Gentle and Humble in Heart
lessons.hear:
Ya had a quick temper, and she often said, “I’m just direct; I don’t mean any harm.” But the people around her said that talking with her felt like stepping on a land mine. She didn’t want to be like this, but she didn’t know how to change.

Jesus invites all who are weary: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matt 11:29) He is not asking us to become gentle through effort, but to “learn from me,” and be slowly shaped by staying near him.

Gentleness is not weakness. Jesus is the Lord of the universe, yet he treats people in the gentlest way: to the weary, he invites them to come; sinners he does not look down on; and to the wicked, he also speaks the truth. Gentleness is having strength but not using it to hurt people.

To learn from Jesus is to spend time before him every day, letting his heart slowly become our heart.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is gentle and humble in heart, yet he has authority. The Bible is my standard: learn from me, and you will find rest for your souls. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me the fruit of gentleness. A life of self uses strength to press people down; a selfless person learns gentleness under the yoke of Christ. May we learn from him every day.
think: According to Matt 11:29, what does Jesus want us to learn from him?
When I speak, do I most often come across as gentle, or sharp?
How much time can I spend today coming to Jesus to learn from him?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are gentle and humble in heart. I am often impatient, and I often hurt people with my words. Take me under your yoke, and teach me to learn from you. Give my heart rest, and let my words carry your gentleness. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, each time before you speak, pause for one second and say in your heart, “Lord, your way.” And try to change one sentence that would have been sharp into a gentler way of saying it.
lessons.quick: Gentleness is strength that doesn’t hurt; learn it from Jesus.
text: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie got into an argument with a coworker over a report, and the more he said, the louder he got, and the other person grew more and more agitated. Finally, a friend said softly, “Let’s have some water first, and then talk it over slowly.” The whole atmosphere eased at once.

Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Prov 15:1) The power of tone often outweighs the content. The same sentence, said gently, is an invitation; said angrily, it is an attack.

Some people say, “I’m right, so I can be loud.” But gentleness is not giving up the truth; it is speaking the truth in a loving way.

Especially in conflict, we can first take a deep breath, lower our volume, slow our pace, acknowledge the other person’s feelings, and only then share our own view.

But if the other person is violent, threatening, or out of control, gentle words may not calm them. At that point, we can leave and seek help.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: when reviled he did not answer back, yet he also spoke when it was time to speak. The Bible is my standard: a gentle answer turns away wrath. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me self-control. A life of self fights over who is louder; a selfless person lets love have the last word. May love have the last word.
think: According to Prov 15:1, what power does a gentle answer have?
What tone do I use most often in conflict?
What gentle word can I use today to defuse a possible conflict?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when I am angry, make me stop first. Give me a gentle answer that turns away wrath. Let me speak not to win, but out of love. If there is danger, lead me away and protect me. Amen.
lessons.do: If a conflict arises today, first take a deep breath, lower your voice, and say, “I hear you saying…, do you feel that…?” Then share your own view. If the other person is violent or threatening, leave first and seek help.
lessons.quick: A gentle answer turns away wrath; if there is danger, protect yourself first.
text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.title: Restore Others in a Spirit of Gentleness
lessons.hear:
Cheng found out that a good friend in his small group had recently been doing something that did not please God. He struggled inside: Should I say something? Would it damage the friendship? If I don’t, I fear he will sink deeper.

Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Gal 6:1) The goal of restoring is repair, not condemnation. The way is gentleness, the attitude is humility, because we ourselves can fall too.

Someone who restores others first examines themselves: Am I acting out of love, or out of comparison? Do I want to help him, or prove I am better than he is?

In practice: talk in private, listen first and speak later, bring Scripture and love, and when needed ask a pastor or a companion to come along.

If the other person’s behavior involves violence, abuse, or illegal acts, this goes beyond what a friend can restore, and professionals and organizations need to step in.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: to Peter who fell, he gently asked three times, “Do you love me?” The Bible is my standard: restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me humble, so that I don’t look down on people. A selfless person doesn’t judge from a high place, but bends down to lift someone up. May we always remember our own limits.
think: According to Gal 6:1, in what spirit are we to restore someone? What should we watch out for?
Do I have a friend who needs to be restored? What is my motive?
How can I speak to him privately and gently?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for gently restoring me. Make me humble, so that I don’t look down on those who have fallen. Give me wisdom to know how to speak and when, and help me watch myself so that I am not tempted. If a situation is beyond my ability, lead me to seek help. Amen.
lessons.do: Pray for a friend you care about who is struggling, and arrange to meet or talk privately, first asking, “How have you been lately?” Just listen, without rushing to give opinions.
lessons.quick: Restoring means being gentle, humble, and knowing your own limits.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Servant Is Gentle Toward All
lessons.hear:
Jing saw online that a friend had posted a view different from her faith, and she couldn’t help leaving a comment underneath, getting more and more worked up as she wrote. In the end, they parted on bad terms, and the friend blocked her.

Paul says to Timothy, “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth.” (2 Tim 2:24–25) Quarreling often only wins the argument but loses the person.

Notice the last sentence: “Perhaps God may give them repentance.” Repentance is God’s work, not ours. What we are to do is be gentle, patient, and able to teach, and leave the result to God.

This applies as well to conflicts in love and relationships: the goal is not to win the debate but to preserve the relationship and the truth. We hold to the truth, but our tone can be gentle.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: facing challenges, he often used questions and parables to lead people to think. The Bible is my standard: the Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he is the Spirit who leads people to repentance. A selfless person doesn’t need to win the argument or prove themselves, and hands the work to the Holy Spirit.
think: According to 2 Tim 2:24–25, how is the Lord’s servant to treat people?
In a debate, do I want more to win, or more to win the person?
How can I express my convictions today in a gentle way?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often want to win the argument and lose the person. Make me gentle and patient, able to teach, and not quarrelsome. I hand to you the matter of others’ repentance; be gracious to them, and make me a vessel you can use. Amen.
lessons.do: If you meet someone today who disagrees with you, try asking just one question: “Why do you think so?” Then listen all the way through without arguing, and share your view in one gentle sentence.
lessons.quick: Don’t quarrel, just be gentle; repentance is God’s work.
text: The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,

lessons.title: Let Your Gentleness Be Known to All
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: learning gentleness from Jesus (Matt 11:29); a gentle answer turns away wrath (Prov 15:1); restoring others gently (Gal 6:1); being gentle toward all (2 Tim 2:24–25).

Paul says, “Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.” (Phil 4:5) The word for “gentleness” can also be translated as mildness or forbearance. Paul hoped that the church would be known before the world as people of gentleness.

He also gives the reason: “The Lord is at hand.” We don’t have to rush to defend ourselves or rush to win, because the Lord is right beside us, and he is the righteous judge.

This week, where did I see my own self-centeredness? Was it impatience, quarreling, or wanting to control? How did God hold me up with his gentleness?

Gentleness is a kind of trust: because we believe the Lord reigns, we don’t have to hold on tightly.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, gentle and humble in heart; the Bible is my standard, a gentle answer turns away wrath; the Holy Spirit is my guide, giving me the fruit of gentleness. Let Jesus be King, and glory to God. Give thanks in everything, and give the glory to Jesus, because all of it is grace accomplished by God.
think: This week, where did I see my own self?
According to Phil 4:5, what are we to let everyone know? Why?
On what occasion next week will I especially let people see my gentleness?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that your gentleness gives me rest. I admit I am often impatient and want to control. Let my gentleness be seen by all. I know the Lord is at hand, and I will hand everything to you. All glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal: my least gentle moment this week; how God held me up. Then choose someone you were ungentle toward, and say, “I’m sorry, and from now on I’ll try to be more gentle.”
lessons.quick: The Lord is at hand; I don’t need to hurry to win, only to be gentle.
text: Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.

weeks.keyText: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.

weeks.title: Self-Control
weeks.theme: Self-control is not suppressing your feelings. It is building a wall around your heart so that love has a safe place to live.
group: Read Prov 25:28. In your dating life or friendships, what does a “city without walls” look like?
Under which emotion do you lose self-control most easily: anger, loneliness, anxiety, or the longing to be noticed?
Which wall do you want to repair this week? Ask a partner to pray for you and to check in on your progress.
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a spiritual partner of the same sex and each say in one sentence: “The moment I lose control most easily is…” Pray for each other, and agree on a day to message each other about your progress. Then send one sentence to a friend: May God give you a heart that is strong, loving, and disciplined.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, run a “wall-building experiment”: pick the situation where you lose control most often (for example, scrolling your phone late at night, or replying to messages in the middle of an argument), write down three rules for yourself in advance, and ask a friend to be your witness. On Sunday evening, review together: which rule held? Which one needs adjusting?

lessons.title: The One Who Cannot Rule His Own Heart
lessons.hear:
Every time Kai argued with his girlfriend, the words were out of his mouth before he could take them back: dredging up old grievances, saying harsh things, and regretting it afterward. He said, “I just can’t control myself.” The Bible describes this condition with a picture: a person who doesn’t rule his own spirit is “like a city that is broken down and without walls.” (Prov 25:28) In ancient times, a city’s wall was its protection. When the wall fell, anything could break in, and nothing could be kept safe.

Self-control is not suppressing your feelings; it is building a wall around your heart. Feelings may come, but not every feeling should immediately become an action. Dating especially needs this wall, because emotions, desires, and expectations are all at their peak.

A wall is not built in a day. First recognize which section of your wall has fallen, then repair it brick by brick.

You don’t need to become perfect overnight. You only need to start today, and at the moment you are most likely to lose control, give yourself one more pause.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in the wilderness and in Gethsemane, he was not led around by his emotions. The Bible is my standard: a heart without walls cannot keep anything safe. The Holy Spirit is my guide: self-control is the fruit of the Spirit, not something I grit my teeth and force through willpower. The life of self is led around by feelings; the selfless life lets Christ rule within.
think: What does Prov 25:28 compare a person without self-control to?
Which section of my “wall” falls most easily: my emotions, my mouth, my phone, or my time?
Which small section of the wall can I begin repairing today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I admit that my heart often has no walls, and I follow a feeling the moment it arrives. Forgive me, and ask the Holy Spirit to grow the fruit of self-control in me, so that even when my emotions run highest, I remember to come to you first. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify the moment when you are most likely to lose control, and write one sentence: “In that moment, the first thing I will do is…” For example, take a deep breath first, pray first, or walk away for ten minutes. Put it on your phone’s home screen.
lessons.quick: Self-control is not suppression; it is building a wall around the heart.
text: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

lessons.title: Guard Your Heart
lessons.hear:
Ayi realized that before even dating anyone, she had already imagined in her mind his name, the wedding, and the children. It startled her. “I haven’t said it out loud, and I haven’t done anything. Is this a problem?”

Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Prov 4:23) The heart is the source; words, actions, and choices all flow from it. To guard is not to forbid feelings, but to watch the entrance: what deserves to move in, and what needs to stop at the door.

The way to guard is very concrete: notice what you keep thinking about, watching, and listening to; and often tell your heart’s concerns to God, and to a trustworthy partner as well. When the heart is lit up, it is less easily carried away.

Guarding is not the same as closing yourself off. The more you hide something in your heart that you dare not say, the more easily it leads you around; bring it into the light, and it no longer has as much power.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his thoughts and intentions were all in the Father’s hands. The Bible is my standard: guard your heart above all else. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lights up the most private corners of my heart. Live from the heart and rely on the Spirit, not on the mind and on self; with the Lord in my heart, I will have joy. With the Lord in my heart, I am not afraid of being exposed to the light.
think: What does Prov 4:23 say is the reason to guard the heart?
What thoughts or images have been occupying my heart again and again lately?
Which concern can I entrust to God and to a partner?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you know all the thoughts, desires, and fears in my heart. Light up my heart, forgive me where I have let myself drift, and make me willing to tell the truth. Holy Spirit, guard the entrance for me, so that my heart is filled with your peace. Amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, spend five minutes writing down the strongest thought in your heart today, then entrust it to God, and circle whether you need to talk about it with a partner.
lessons.quick: Guard your heart; everything you do in life flows from it.
text: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

lessons.title: Not Timid, but Strong, Loving, and Disciplined
lessons.hear:
Zhe’s impression of self-control was suppression: you can’t think, can’t want, can’t speak, as if you were tying yourself up. The tighter he tied, the more he lost control the moment he loosened his grip.

Paul said to Timothy, “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Tim 1:7) The heart God gives has three sides. Strength helps me dare to speak the truth and to refuse. Love makes me use my strength to love people, not to control them. Discipline gives me a sense of proportion, so I know when to stop.

Self-control, then, is not fear; it is love with strength. It is not about locking yourself away, but about learning how to use yourself well.

Zhe began to practice: when angry, he stops to pray first and then speaks; when longing for attention, he first goes before God to be loved, and then goes to find people. He said this is not less freedom, but more strength.

Which one do you want to practice today: strength, love, or discipline?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was both strong and loving, both free and measured. The Bible is my standard: what God gave is not a timid heart. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives strength, love, and discipline. The life of self is either indulgent or suppressed; the selfless life is filled with the Holy Spirit and so has power.
think: What kind of heart does 2 Tim 1:7 say God gave us?
Is my impression of self-control suppression, fear, or love with strength?
Which area (strength, love, or discipline) most needs strengthening today?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me not a timid heart. Make me strong, so I dare to speak the truth and to refuse; make me loving, so I use my strength to love others; make me disciplined, so I know where to draw the line. Fill me with your Holy Spirit. Amen. And hold me up when I am weak.
lessons.do: Pick the one you lack most among strength, love, and discipline, and do one concrete small thing today: for example, dare to say one true thing you didn’t want to say, or reach out to care for someone, or end your phone scrolling ten minutes earlier.
lessons.quick: What God gave is a heart of strength, love, and discipline, not a timid heart.
text: For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

lessons.title: Your Body Is the Temple of the Holy Spirit
lessons.hear:
Xiao’an said, “It’s my body, so I decide for myself.” A friend at the other extreme said, “My body belongs to my future spouse.” The Bible doesn’t fully agree with either statement.

Paul said, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.” (1 Cor 6:19–20) Our bodies were bought by Christ with his life, and are the temple where the Holy Spirit lives. This statement does not give anyone else authority over your body; it fixes your dignity in Christ.

For this reason, no one has the right, in the name of love, to force, coax, or control your body. Self-control is my choice to use my body to glorify God; being violated is not your sin, and you may refuse, and you may ask for help.

Your worth does not lie in who chooses you or who admires you, but in the fact that Christ has already paid the price for you. Starting from here, you can freely say yes, and also say no.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his body was broken for us, and he also protected the weak. The Bible is my standard: the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, not someone else’s possession. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lives in me. The life of self says, “It’s my body, my call”; the selfless life says, “I already belong to Christ, so I want to honor him.”
think: According to 1 Cor 6:19–20, why are we not our own?
How have I viewed my body in the past: with contempt, with shame, or as precious?
How can I glorify God with my body today (rest, exercise, refusing, eating)?
lessons.speak: Jesus, thank you for buying me with your life; my body is the temple of the Holy Spirit. Heal my shame and contempt toward my body, and protect me from being violated by anyone. Help me glorify you with my body. Amen. And help me say no with dignity in front of others.
lessons.do: Today, do one respectful thing for your body: eat a good meal, go to bed early, take a walk, or say no to an invitation that makes you uncomfortable. If you have ever been violated, talk with someone you trust or with a professional counselor.
lessons.quick: My body belongs to Christ, and my dignity is a gift from him.
text: Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

lessons.title: Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak
lessons.hear:
This week we talked about self-control: building a wall around the heart, guarding the heart, being strong, loving, and disciplined, and the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit. In the end it comes down to the mouth and the ears. When Xiaolin argued with her boyfriend, she always cut him off before he finished: “I know what you’re going to say!” The result was an even fiercer fight.

James says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19) To be swift to hear is to be willing to understand first; to be slow to speak is to think before the words come out. If the other person’s words are already humiliation or a threat, protecting yourself is the priority.

This week’s lessons have all been practicing one and the same thing: letting the Holy Spirit rule within me so that I am not led around by emotions, desires, and words. Self-control does not come from trying twice as hard, but from leaning more deeply.

Looking back on this week, ask yourself: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, he listened to people patiently; the Bible is my standard, be swift to hear, slow to speak; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he bears the fruit of self-control. The life of self rushes to talk and hurries to argue; the selfless life listens first, then speaks. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up in my weakness this week?
Which wall will I keep repairing next week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for this week’s illumination. Forgive my self-centeredness, and thank you for holding me up. Teach me to be swift to hear and slow to speak, and when I am humiliated or threatened, give me the wisdom and courage to walk away. Glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week, the wall I repaired, and one thing I need a partner to hold me accountable for; then send one of those sentences to your spiritual partner.
lessons.quick: Listen to the end, then speak; look back on the week, and see both your self and God’s support.
text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

weeks.keyText: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.
